09.15:
Did-you-mean suggests a corrected query when the typed text may contain an error. It should preserve user intent rather than always choosing the nearest dictionary word. A proper name, product code, or new brand may look misspelled to a general dictionary. The service must generate plausible candidates, rank them in context, and decide whether to show a suggestion or search with it automatically.

## Generate candidates efficiently

Edit distance counts insertions, deletions, substitutions, and sometimes transpositions needed to change one string into another. Comparing a query token against every term in a large vocabulary is expensive. A k-gram index maps short character sequences to vocabulary terms that share them; use it to narrow candidates, then compute edit distance on that small set. Stanford's retrieval text describes both methods. Limit correction distance by token length: changing one character in a three-letter word is much riskier than in a fifteen-letter word.

Index corpus terms or a curated query vocabulary with frequencies. Corpus frequency alone can prefer a common but irrelevant word; query-log frequency can include repeated typos. Add a domain dictionary for product names, acronyms, and identifiers. A candidate should remain compatible with the user's language and keyboard layout. For multiword queries, generate only a bounded number of alternatives per token to avoid combinatorial explosion.

## Rank whole-query meaning

Context can distinguish `form` from `from` in a phrase even though both are valid words. Evaluate the likelihood of the complete corrected phrase using term co-occurrence, language-model evidence, or actual search result quality. Elasticsearch offers term and phrase suggesters for these different stages. Keep the original query's strong matches as evidence against changing it. A correction that yields many results is not automatically better; those results may all be off topic.

Choose presentation based on confidence. For a low-confidence alternative, show “Did you mean ...?” as a link and retain original results. For a high-confidence correction of a zero-result query, a product may search the corrected form but clearly say so and offer a way to return to the original. Never silently alter an exact SKU, quoted phrase, or person name. Preserve both typed and effective queries in the result context so pagination and analytics use the same interpretation.

## Evaluate and operate the feature

Create test queries with typos, valid rare terms, multilingual words, names, and identifiers. Measure correction precision, missed corrections, result quality after correction, and user acceptance. False corrections are particularly costly because they can hide the intended target. Monitor latency and candidate count; spelling work should not make every ordinary search slow. Cache frequent corrections with an analyzer and vocabulary version in the key.

When the vocabulary changes, refresh correction data alongside the search index. A new product name should not be “corrected” to an older competitor. Store only the query data needed to improve correction, with appropriate privacy controls and retention. An explainable candidate list makes it easier to diagnose an embarrassing suggestion before it becomes a repeated user experience.

## Design review

How are candidates generated and bounded? Which exact strings are protected? What evidence chooses a whole-phrase correction? When does the UI auto-search versus offer a link? How are false corrections measured and rolled back?

09.16:
Related searches offer alternative queries after a user has searched. They can broaden a topic, narrow an intent, or help recover from poor results. They are different from autocomplete, which starts with a prefix, and from spelling correction, which tries to repair a likely error. A useful related query should lead to a distinct, relevant result set rather than repeat the same words in another order.

## Generate several kinds of candidates

Query-session transitions can reveal refinements: users who searched `running shoes` may next search `trail running shoes`. Co-occurrence is evidence, not proof of a good suggestion; a frequent transition can reflect frustration. Content-based generation can find nearby terms from documents retrieved for the original query. A curated taxonomy can add predictable refinements such as category, brand, or location. Embedding similarity can find paraphrases, but paraphrases that return nearly identical results add little value.

Store each candidate's normalized text, source, query class, locale, and supporting counts or confidence. Exclude sensitive or personally identifying queries from mined suggestions. Apply a minimum support threshold and moderation policy before showing log-derived phrases. A new topic may have no log history, so fall back to taxonomy or corpus-driven candidates rather than returning an empty box.

## Rank for usefulness and diversity

Score candidates for topical relation, evidence quality, and expected result quality. Then diversify: one broadening, one narrowing, and one adjacent intent may be more useful than five near duplicates. Check each candidate against the current index so it does not lead to zero results or only unavailable items. For an exact-ID query, related searches may be inappropriate; show similar products or documentation links under a different label instead of implying the ID was wrong.

Keep a clear boundary between personalization and global suggestions. A user's recent search may improve their own suggestions, but it should not leak into another user's page. For multi-tenant products, filter candidate sources and result checks by tenant and permissions. Cache only when the context key includes the constraints that affect validity. Invalidate or expire suggestions when the underlying corpus changes substantially.

## Evaluate the destination, not the click

Measure suggestion selection, subsequent search success, reformulation loops, and the quality of destination results. A related phrase can earn clicks because it looks interesting while leading to an irrelevant page. Offline review should include candidate diversity and result-set overlap. Test popular and long-tail queries, new content, sensitive query classes, and locales. Stanford's query-expansion discussion provides the retrieval foundation; a product-facing related-search system adds session evidence, filtering, and presentation decisions.

Log why a suggestion was shown: taxonomy edge, aggregate transition, or content similarity. This supports debugging and moderation. Limit the number shown and the computation budget; a slow suggestion panel should never delay the main results. If the recommendation pipeline is unavailable, omit the panel and keep search functional.

## Design review

What relationship should each suggestion express? Are mined queries frequent and safe enough to show? Does the destination have useful results? Are tenant and personal contexts isolated? How will repeated reformulation loops be detected?

09.17:
Recent searches help a user repeat or continue their own queries. The feature is a small history store with product and privacy semantics, not merely a list in a search box. Decide whether history is per device, per account, or both; how long it persists; which queries are excluded; and whether deleting an entry removes it from every device. A local-only implementation is simpler, while account sync requires server storage and conflict handling.

## Define the stored record

Store normalized query text for deduplication, original display text, time, optional filters, and an opaque account or device scope. A user who searches `boots` with category `hiking` may expect that filter to return when reopening the query; include only filters that can be restored safely. Keep a bounded list, such as the most recent N entries, and update an existing query's timestamp rather than creating many duplicates. Exact query history can reveal health, finances, or identity, so collect less than a general analytics log might collect.

For device-only history, browser storage can retain a bounded list without a backend. MDN documents that `localStorage` persists across browsing sessions for an origin; that also means another person using the same browser profile may see it. Offer a clear delete action and consider session-only storage for a privacy-sensitive surface. For signed-in history, store server-side with authorization on every read and write, encryption and retention appropriate to the data, and a deletion path that reaches replicas and caches.

## Resolve synchronization and identity changes

When a user signs in, decide whether anonymous device history merges into the account or remains local. A shared device can make automatic merge surprising, so treat it as a product decision. When signed in on two devices, merge by query key and latest timestamp, then cap the list. Use server time or tolerate clock skew so one bad device clock does not pin an entry forever. Signing out should stop showing account history to the next user, even if a local UI cache remains.

Deletion must be specific. Removing one entry should not reappear after an offline device syncs an older copy. A tombstone or versioned deletion can prevent resurrection until all clients have converged; a short-lived local-only store can simply clear itself. A “clear all” action should explain its scope, for example this device or all devices. Do not rely on a front-end hide operation if the backend continues to return the data.

## Make the feature useful and measurable

Show recent searches only when the input is empty or when they are clearly distinguished from live autocomplete. Preserve keyboard navigation and a remove control that is accessible. Do not place a private history item in a global suggestion index. If an old query now has no results, normal search should still handle it; recent history is a shortcut, not a result guarantee.

Measure use of recent entries, delete actions, sync failures, and stale entries without logging more sensitive text than necessary. Test multiple devices, sign-out, browser storage limits, private browsing, and deletion while offline. The feature should degrade gracefully when history storage is unavailable: searching must still work.

## Design review

Is history scoped to a device or account? Which query details are stored, and for how long? What happens on sign-in and sign-out? Can an offline client resurrect a deleted query? Does the UI distinguish private history from public suggestions?

10.01:
Counting sounds like a single integer increment, but high write rate, retries, time windows, and distinct-user semantics make it a system-design problem. Start by naming the thing being counted. Total accepted events, unique users, billable actions, and a number displayed on a page can require different guarantees. A financial or quota counter may need exact, transactional accounting; a public popularity badge may tolerate lag and small approximation.

## Define an event and its identity

For exact counting, give each accepted action a stable event ID. A request retry or broker redelivery should not add twice. One approach stores an event row with a unique ID and increments an aggregate in the same transaction. Another keeps the event log authoritative and derives a materialized count asynchronously. The first offers immediate exactness at the database boundary but can create contention; the second scales writes and enables replay but shows a lagging view.

Define the dimensions before building the key: `item_id`, event type, tenant, and bucket time might all matter. A counter labeled “today” needs a time zone and a rule for late events. If the event's timestamp comes from an untrusted client, it can put counts in the wrong window; use a server timestamp or a validated event-time policy. Store enough raw evidence to reconcile a derived count after a bug.

## Avoid one hot row

An atomic database increment serializes updates on one row. At modest throughput that simplicity is valuable. At high throughput, partition events or use counter shards keyed by `(item_id, shard_id)` and sum them for reads. A popular item's writes spread across shards, but reading the exact total becomes more expensive and a shard failure may make the total temporarily incomplete. Batch increments from workers to reduce write frequency; then quantify how many increments could be lost if a worker crashes before flushing.

Redis `INCR` is atomic on one key and can serve a fast approximate display counter, but durability and reconciliation depend on Redis configuration and the write path. Do not use a cache number as the sole authority for billable actions. A stream processor can aggregate events by key into a state store and publish updates to a read model; Kafka Streams documents keyed `count` and stateful aggregation. If processing is replayable, rebuild the read model from the source log.

## Make accuracy visible

State whether the count is exact, eventually exact, or estimated. A UI can show a rounded count while a back-office report uses reconciled exact totals. Measure accepted events, deduplicated events, aggregation lag, missing partitions, count drift against raw events, and read latency. A counter that looks smooth while its event consumer is stopped is not healthy.

For very large distinct counts, a HyperLogLog sketch trades exactness for bounded memory. That is a different question from counting every event: one user producing ten events increases total events by ten but unique users by one. Keep the two measures separate in names, schema, and dashboards. Choose the simplest counter that meets the actual accuracy and freshness requirements.

## Design review

What exactly increments the count? Which ID makes retries safe? Is the displayed number allowed to lag? Where is the authoritative event record? What contention or hot key appears under the most popular item, and how is drift detected?

10.02:
A view counter measures how often content is viewed, but “view” needs a product definition. A page request, a rendered page, a visible item for a minimum duration, and a unique person per day produce different numbers. Bots, reloads, prefetching, and retries can inflate raw requests. Define the event at the client and server boundary before scaling the counter; otherwise a highly available pipeline only computes a misleading value quickly.

## Capture a defensible view event

For a video, a view might require playback beyond a threshold; for an article, meaningful visibility or dwell may matter. Give the client an event ID and include content ID, session or anonymous viewer scope, event time, and a version of the view rule. Validate the event on the server. Do not trust an arbitrary client count or timestamp for a billable metric. Apply bot and abuse filters with documented limits; those filters may change, so retain enough raw data to recompute affected periods.

Duplicates arise when a client retries, a queue redelivers, or a user reloads. Decide whether each reload is a new view or whether a session/time-window rule deduplicates it. A bounded deduplication table keyed by event ID prevents transport duplicates. A separate `(viewer, content, window)` key can enforce a product-level unique-view rule. These keys serve different purposes and should not be conflated.

## Absorb hot content traffic

Writing every view into one content row creates a hotspot for a viral item. Append validated events to a durable stream, partition by content ID or a salted variant, and aggregate in short intervals. If one content ID is still too hot, salt the key into several subcounters and sum them. The read path can show the latest aggregate plus recent increments, or accept a short delay. Make the freshness window visible in internal metrics even if the public display rounds the number.

Bucket events by a defined clock. Event time reflects when the view happened; processing time reflects when the system received it. Mobile clients may send late events after reconnecting. Apache Beam's windowing documentation describes watermarks and allowed lateness: decide when a daily count becomes final and how late corrections are applied. If a public count must never move backward, keep that as a display policy rather than corrupting the accurate underlying count.

## Separate display, reporting, and billing

A public “1.2M views” badge can be cached and rounded. An analytics dashboard may need hourly breakdowns with a revision marker. An advertising report requires stronger event validation, deduplication, auditability, and reconciliation. Do not assume one materialized integer satisfies all three. Retain raw events under a bounded policy and derive multiple views from the same definition version.

Measure ingestion loss, duplicate rate, bot-filter rate, per-content skew, aggregation lag, and drift between raw accepted events and aggregates. Load-test a single viral content ID as well as total traffic. If a stream partition is unavailable, the system should have a clear choice between delaying the view count and dropping a noncritical event; silently claiming exactness after loss is worse than admitting approximation.

## Design review

What user action counts as a view? How are transport duplicates and repeated genuine views distinguished? What happens for one viral item? When does a time bucket become final? Which count is safe for billing versus display?

10.03:
An impression is an opportunity for a person to see an item. In feeds and advertising, a server returning an item is not necessarily the same as the item becoming visible on screen. The product must specify the visibility threshold, duration, and measurement method. Counting the wrong point in the pipeline can make an experiment or billing report look precise while measuring delivery rather than exposure.

## Place the event at the right boundary

The server can log a served impression when it includes an item in a response. A client can log a viewable impression when the item enters the viewport for a required interval. Both are useful, but label them separately. Client observations can be lost when a tab closes, blocked by network conditions, or fabricated by automated clients. Include a server-issued request ID, placement ID, item ID, position, experiment assignment, and a unique impression ID so the server can validate context and deduplicate retries.

Virtualized lists and infinite scroll complicate measurement. An item may be prefetched but never rendered, rendered offscreen, or seen twice after scrolling away and back. Decide whether repeated exposure in one session counts again and enforce that rule in the event identity. Keep a version of the visibility logic because a change from “one pixel visible” to “half visible for one second” changes the metric even if the data pipeline is unchanged.

## Aggregate without losing auditability

Send accepted events to a durable log and partition them for processing. Count by item, placement, campaign, and time bucket as needed. High-cardinality dimensions can explode storage, so choose a small set of materialized aggregates and query raw events for less common breakdowns. Use event IDs to avoid duplicate counts after worker retries. A windowed stream processor can update minute and hour buckets; late arrivals require correction or a declared cutoff.

For advertising, keep an immutable accepted-event record and a reconciliation trail from served to viewable to billable impressions. A dropped client event should not be converted silently into a billable exposure. Billing rules may require additional fraud filtering and contractual definitions outside the counter itself. Public dashboards can be eventual, while financial reports need a reproducible close process with revisions recorded.

## Use the metric carefully

Impressions are often the denominator for click-through rate. If a UI change alters which impressions are reported, CTR can move without any change in user interest. Track served, rendered, and viewable counts, plus client event delivery rate, by platform and app version. Compare experiment groups on the same instrumentation. A ranker trained on clicks without impression and position data will learn exposure bias from the current ranking.

Monitor event lag, duplicate rate, client-to-server delivery loss, bot filtering, and impossible ratios such as more clicks than validated impressions. Test scroll, rapid navigation, offline replay, and browser backgrounding. A metric definition should include examples of what counts and what does not so engineering, analytics, and product teams share the same meaning.

## Design review

Is the metric served, rendered, viewable, or billable? Which ID deduplicates transport retries? How do repeated exposures count? Can a client fabricate the event? How are late events and instrumentation changes reflected in reports?

10.04:
HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct values in a stream using far less memory than storing every value. It is useful for questions such as “how many unique viewers saw this page today?” where a small statistical error is acceptable. It cannot list the viewers, enforce a one-per-user quota, or prove an exact billing count. Name the result an estimate and keep its error properties visible.

## Understand the sketch intuition

Hash each identifier into a uniform bit string. Rare patterns of leading zero bits become more likely as more distinct identifiers are observed. HyperLogLog divides hashes into registers, records an extremal pattern in each, and combines register values into a cardinality estimate with bias corrections. Repeating the same identifier normally does not change the sketch because it hashes to the same value. The hash quality and stable normalization of identifiers matter: `User-7` and `user-7` are distinct unless the product normalizes them first.

Redis exposes `PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`, and `PFMERGE` for its HyperLogLog implementation and documents sub-1% standard error for that implementation. A standard error is not a hard maximum error on every estimate. For a small set where exactness matters, use a set or exact table instead. Some implementations use a sparse representation for small cardinalities, but the API still returns an estimate with implementation-specific behavior.

## Merge by the right dimensions

Create one sketch per day and segment, then merge compatible sketches to estimate a week or a broader segment. Merging requires the same hash function, precision, and identifier definition. Summing daily unique-user estimates is wrong when one user appears on multiple days; merge the sketches to count the union. Similarly, summing country sketches is only valid for an event count, not for globally unique users who may appear in several countries.

Sketches are easy to add to and merge, but removing one identifier is not generally supported. If a user deletion or fraud correction must subtract past membership, rebuild the affected bucket from raw events or use a different data structure. Windowing means storing separate sketches for bounded intervals and expiring them under a retention policy. Define how late events update an already published bucket and whether a reported number can be revised.

## Validate and operate estimates

Compare HLL estimates with exact distinct counts on sampled buckets and at several cardinalities. Monitor relative error, empty and low-count behavior, hash/version mismatches, and merge failures. A broken identifier extraction step can change the count much more than the sketch's statistical error. For example, hashing a session ID instead of a user ID measures sessions, regardless of how accurate the HLL algorithm is.

Use the same input event deduplication policy across exact and approximate reports. HyperLogLog naturally ignores repeated identical identifiers within a bucket, but it does not decide whether two accounts belong to one person or whether a bot should be excluded. Keep the semantic definition of “distinct” separate from the implementation. When reports are high stakes, preserve raw data and use an exact close process.

## Design review

What identifier defines uniqueness? Is an estimate acceptable for this decision? Are sketches merged instead of summed across overlapping groups? What happens when a record must be removed? How will estimate error and identifier-pipeline errors be detected?

10.05:
A mergeable sketch is a compact summary that can be combined with another compatible summary to approximate a result over their union. This property lets workers analyze partitions independently and then reduce their summaries, without shipping every raw event to one machine. The merge operation must have a defined mathematical meaning; simply adding two estimates is often wrong, especially for distinct counts and percentiles.

## Match the sketch to the question

HyperLogLog estimates distinct identifiers and can merge registers for a union. A count-min sketch estimates per-key frequencies and can combine compatible counter tables. Quantile sketches summarize a value distribution so percentiles can be queried after merging. Frequent-items sketches seek likely heavy hitters. These are different contracts: a distinct-count sketch cannot answer “which users?” and a quantile sketch cannot provide an exact sum. Apache DataSketches documents several sketch families and a feature matrix for union, intersection, and merge support.

Before selecting one, state the error bound or empirical accuracy target, memory per partition, update rate, merge frequency, and needed operations. Some sketches support only union, while others support set intersections or differences. Some accept weighted updates or deletions; many do not. A design that requires retracting fraudulent events may need raw replay or a different summary.

## Keep versions and dimensions compatible

Suppose each region maintains a daily unique-viewer sketch. A global daily estimate comes from merging sketches built with the same identifier normalization, hash function, precision, and bucket definition. If one region hashes account IDs and another hashes device IDs, the merge is technically possible but semantically invalid. Store sketch type, parameters, schema version, time window, and input definition with each serialized value. Reject incompatible merges rather than returning a plausible but wrong number.

Sketches can be merged hierarchically: worker → region → global. This reduces network transfer and spreads CPU work. Merging should be associative enough for the implementation's documented guarantee, so a retry or different merge tree does not materially change the result beyond expected error. Deduplicate partition snapshots or use versioned replacements; merging the same sketch twice can double frequency estimates for additive sketches, even if a distinct-count union is insensitive to repeated identical members.

## Publish estimates responsibly

Expose an estimate and its uncertainty or expected error, not a falsely precise integer. Validate against exact calculations on sampled or smaller buckets. Check low-cardinality behavior, skew, serialization compatibility, and memory growth. Keep raw events for a bounded period when exact audit or rebuilding matters. A sketch reduces the cost of a question, but it does not repair lost input events or a wrong event definition.

Plan time windows explicitly. A daily sketch cannot answer an arbitrary rolling 24-hour query exactly unless the system keeps finer buckets or accepts boundary error. Merging monthly and daily sketches with overlapping intervals double counts frequency metrics. Track provenance and window IDs so the query planner merges disjoint, compatible inputs. The power of mergeability is parallelism with a known approximation contract.

## Design review

Which exact question and operation must the sketch support? What error is acceptable? Are input identities and parameters identical across partitions? Can duplicate merges or overlapping windows corrupt the answer? How will an old sketch be rebuilt after a bug?

10.06:
Bucketed aggregation groups events into time intervals before computing counts, sums, or sketches. It makes dashboards and retention manageable: a query for yesterday's hourly traffic reads 24 buckets rather than every request. The hard choices are which clock defines the bucket, how late data changes a result, and whether a displayed aggregate is provisional or final.

## Choose event time or processing time

Event time is when the action occurred. Processing time is when the pipeline handled it. A phone can record a purchase at 10:02 and deliver it at 10:15 after reconnecting. Event-time aggregation puts it in the 10:00 bucket; processing-time aggregation puts it in the 10:15 bucket. For business reporting, event time often matches the question, but client timestamps must be validated. For infrastructure alerting, processing time may be more appropriate. Apache Beam distinguishes these clocks and uses watermarks as estimates of event-time completeness.

Define interval boundaries precisely: `[10:00, 10:05)` includes the start but excludes the end. Use UTC internally and convert to the report's time zone at the edge. A “day” in a local time zone can be 23 or 25 hours around daylight-saving changes. Never derive daily totals by assuming every day has 24 fixed UTC hours when the product promises a local calendar day.

## Decide when to emit and revise

A tumbling window emits disjoint buckets; a hopping window overlaps, such as a 15-minute window advancing every minute. A session window groups events separated by no more than a gap and can merge when a late event bridges two sessions. Kafka Streams documents these window types and state stores. A processing engine can emit an early provisional count, an on-time count when the watermark passes, and late corrections for an allowed period. State whether each emission replaces the previous value or is a delta; consumers that add a replacement as a delta will overcount.

Set allowed lateness from observed delivery delay and business needs. If events arrive after the deadline, quarantine them, revise a historical report through a separate path, or drop them with a measured count. No watermark is a proof that no earlier event will ever arrive. Keeping windows open forever grows state, so pair lateness with retention and a reconciliation policy.

## Scale hot keys and query rollups

Partition aggregates by dimension and time. A single global counter can be hot; partial aggregates can be combined after a short interval. Use minute buckets to construct hours and days only when the requested dimensions and semantics are compatible. Distinct users cannot be computed by summing minute distinct counts because a user may appear in several minutes; merge a distinct sketch or revisit raw IDs. Similarly, averaging minute p95 values does not yield an hourly p95.

Monitor watermark lag, late-event rate, state-store size, emitted revisions, bucket drift against raw events, and query cost. Test out-of-order events, duplicates, clock skew, and replay. A dashboard should label provisional data when later corrections are possible, especially if users make decisions from near-real-time numbers.

## Design review

Which clock and time zone define the bucket? Are windows disjoint or overlapping? What happens to late events? Does an output replace or add to prior output? Can larger intervals be derived correctly from smaller ones for this metric?

10.07:
Raw events record individual facts; derived analytics summarize them for fast queries. Both have value. A materialized hourly count is cheap to read but loses detail, while a raw event log can answer new questions and repair mistakes at greater storage and processing cost. The design should state which facts are retained, which reports can be recomputed, and when a report becomes authoritative.

## Define the raw event contract

An event should have a stable ID, type, schema version, subject, event time, ingestion time, and the fields needed for approved analyses. Avoid collecting extra sensitive data merely because storage is cheap. Validate required fields at ingestion and quarantine malformed events rather than silently changing their meaning. Maintain producer ownership and a schema evolution process; a field that switches from cents to dollars without a version will corrupt historical aggregates.

Raw events may arrive twice or out of order. The pipeline needs an idempotency policy based on event ID and a rule for late event-time placement. A log's retention must be long enough for expected recovery and reprocessing. If raw events are deleted for privacy or retention reasons, derived datasets and backups need a corresponding deletion plan. “We can always replay” is false once the source history has expired.

## Materialize useful views

Compute counters, sums, sketches, and grouped rollups for frequent queries. Record the input offset or watermark, transformation version, and output window for each view. A derived table can be updated incrementally from a stream or built in batches from raw storage. Kafka Streams' table and aggregation model illustrates how a stream of changes can maintain a queryable view. Beam's windows and triggers show how early and late results can be emitted for event-time reporting.

Different reports may need different definitions. A public view count can filter bots approximately and update every minute; a financial settlement report may close once with audited rules. Do not hide that distinction under one generic `count` field. Version metric definitions and expose whether a number is preliminary or finalized.

## Recover from a bad transform

When a parser or fraud filter is wrong, create a new derived dataset from raw events using the corrected code. Validate it against the old dataset and known examples, then switch readers or publish a revision. Overwriting the only aggregate in place without provenance makes the change hard to audit. Keep enough source-to-output lineage to explain why a bucket changed. If a real-time pipeline loses a partition, a batch repair can backfill the affected range.

Storage and compute costs need explicit bounds. Keep detailed events for the period needed for audit and correction, then roll up or expire according to policy. Sampled data can support exploratory trends but not exact billing. Monitor ingestion completeness, schema errors, deduplication, consumer lag, raw-to-derived drift, and report query latency. A dashboard with fast queries but no provenance can give confident-looking wrong answers.

## Design review

Which store holds the authoritative fact? How long can raw events be replayed? What versions identify event schema and metric logic? How are late and duplicate events handled? Can an incorrect aggregate be rebuilt and switched without losing recent input?

10.08:
A count-min sketch estimates how often each key appears in a stream while using bounded memory. It stores several hash-indexed counter rows. For each event, it increments one cell in each row; to query a key, it takes the minimum of those cells. Hash collisions can add counts from other keys, so the estimate is normally at least the true frequency for a stream of nonnegative updates. The sketch is useful for frequent keys, not for an exact charge or a precise count of rare events.

## Size the error against total traffic

The width controls collision error and the depth controls the probability that all rows collide badly. Redis exposes initialization by error tolerance and probability, and its documentation notes that low counts beneath the error threshold can be mostly noise. A promise of “0.1% error” is relative to the total stream count, not necessarily 0.1% of each item's count. If there are a billion events, even a small fraction of total traffic can overwhelm a key with only a few true occurrences.

Use a stable, independent set of hash functions or seeds and keep them with the sketch metadata. A query made with a different hash configuration reads unrelated cells. Normalize keys consistently; `Item42` and `item42` count separately unless deliberately canonicalized. Define whether increments may be negative. The textbook nonnegative guarantee does not automatically hold when deletions or corrections are applied through negative updates, even if a particular implementation accepts them.

## Combine shards and windows safely

Workers can maintain compatible sketches for disjoint event partitions and merge corresponding cells. This supports high ingestion rate without a single hot key. Do not merge the same partition snapshot twice if the merge adds counters. Store partition, input range, sketch version, and window so a reducer can detect duplicates. Keep separate sketches for time buckets; a cumulative sketch cannot answer “last ten minutes” unless it has a supported subtraction method or the system retains narrower buckets.

For top products, the sketch can estimate candidate frequencies, but it cannot enumerate every key it has seen. Pair it with a bounded candidate set or a frequent-items algorithm. An exact counter for the top few keys can supplement the sketch and provide a quality check. Querying all possible product IDs to find the maximum defeats the memory advantage if the key universe is large.

## Validate the use case

Compare estimates with exact counts on sampled keys across low, medium, and high frequencies. Monitor total updates, collision-driven overcount, memory, merge completeness, and key distribution changes. A highly skewed hot key can contaminate cells for many rare keys. If an operation needs exact quotas, inventory, or billing, maintain authoritative per-key records and use the sketch only for detection or prioritization.

Count-min sketch is attractive because update and query work are bounded and independent of the number of distinct keys. That benefit comes with a one-sided approximation under its standard assumptions. State those assumptions and expose the estimate as an estimate, especially when a threshold decision has consequences.

## Design review

What is the expected total stream volume and acceptable absolute error for rare keys? Are updates nonnegative? How are hash seeds, partitions, and windows versioned? Can a duplicate merge inflate counts? Does the product need to enumerate heavy hitters or only query known keys?

10.09:
Heavy hitters are keys that contribute a large share of a stream: popular posts, top search queries, or sources of unexpected traffic. A top-K dashboard needs to discover the keys as well as estimate their counts. A count-min sketch can estimate a key you already know, but it cannot list every key it has seen. Use a frequent-items summary, a bounded candidate table, or a partitioned exact aggregation with a merge step.

## Specify the top-K question

“Top ten products today” needs a time zone, accepted-event definition, and tie rule. Decide whether the ranking is by event count, distinct users, revenue, or another weight. A product with one purchase worth a large amount ranks differently under count and revenue. Choose how late events revise the list. If the top-K is used for abuse detection, a short freshness target may matter more than perfect order among close candidates.

For an exact result, aggregate every key in a distributed map, merge partition counts, and sort or maintain a heap. That can be expensive when key cardinality is huge. A frequent-items sketch keeps a bounded set of candidate keys and approximate frequency bounds. Apache DataSketches documents frequent-items error thresholds and modes that trade false positives and negatives. Choose the mode based on whether missing a true heavy hitter is worse than showing an extra candidate.

## Discover candidates under skew

Each partition can keep local candidates, then a reducer merges compatible summaries. A globally frequent key might be only moderately frequent in every partition, so simply taking each partition's top ten can miss it. Local candidate sets must be large enough, or the algorithm must provide a merge guarantee. Once candidates are known, a second pass over retained raw events or exact per-key counters can refine their final ordering. This two-stage design is often worth the cost for an externally visible leaderboard.

Hot keys can create hot stream partitions when partitioned directly by key. Salt their event keys for ingestion, aggregate partial counts, then combine by the original key. Keep the source event IDs and partition ranges so retries do not double-merge a partial summary. A single corrupt or missing partition can distort the ranking; track completeness by input range, not only whether the final reducer ran.

## Make outputs stable and useful

Near-tied items may swap places from small count changes or sketch error. Consider a refresh interval, minimum change threshold, or displaying approximate counts instead of continuously reshuffling the UI. A top-K list should include the measurement window and data freshness. If the purpose is operations, show uncertainty and any incomplete partitions so responders do not mistake a partial stream for a real traffic shift.

Evaluate with exact counts on sampled windows and deliberately skewed synthetic streams. Measure recall of true top-K, rank stability, count error, update throughput, merge latency, and memory. Test a new key that surges suddenly, not only long-established popular keys. The sketch is an optimization for discovery; the product contract decides whether approximate ranks are enough.

## Design review

What weight and window define “top”? Can the method enumerate candidate keys? Could a global heavy hitter be absent from all local top-K lists? Which errors are acceptable? Is there a second exact pass for externally important rankings?

10.10:
Reservoir sampling keeps a fixed-size random sample from a stream whose final length is unknown. It is useful for inspecting events, building an approximate test set, or retaining examples without storing every item. The basic algorithm gives every item seen so far the same probability of being in the sample, provided the random choices are unbiased and every item is processed once. It does not automatically produce a sample of distinct users or a sample weighted by business importance.

## Apply Algorithm R

Keep the first `k` items in a reservoir. For the `i`th item after that, draw a random integer uniformly from `1..i`. If the number is at most `k`, replace that reservoir slot with the new item; otherwise leave the sample unchanged. The new item has inclusion probability `k/i`. An earlier item survives each later replacement with the right probability, so after `n` events every item has probability `k/n` of inclusion. Vitter's original work and Stanford's algorithm notes develop this result.

This method uses O(k) storage and a single pass, but it considers every event. For very high-rate streams, skip-based variants reduce random draws. Use a well-seeded generator and avoid modulo bias if the implementation maps random bits into `1..i`. Record the algorithm version and input count with the sample so the result can be interpreted and reproduced in tests.

## Clarify what the sample represents

If one user generates 100 events and another generates one, an event reservoir is 100 times more likely to include the first user's activity. To sample users uniformly, sample a deduplicated user stream or use a stable hash-priority scheme over user IDs. Similarly, a global reservoir over all traffic may contain almost no examples from a rare but important tenant. Stratify by tenant, geography, error class, or time bucket if those slices matter, and account for the changed inclusion probabilities when estimating population statistics.

Distributed merging needs care. Concatenating two reservoirs or picking half the slots from each biases a sample when partitions have different sizes. Carry each partition's seen count and use a correct weighted merge, or assign each event a random priority and keep the global k smallest priorities across partitions. The latter can be merged by a top-k reduction if priorities are independent and stable. Retries must not give an event a new priority or another chance to enter the sample.

## Handle time and privacy

A cumulative reservoir represents all history and adapts slowly to recent changes. For “last hour” analysis, maintain separate time buckets or use a windowed sampling algorithm. Keep sample payloads small and redact sensitive data; sampling reduces volume, not privacy obligations. If sampled events can be deleted by user request, retain enough identity and provenance to find and remove them. Do not use a reservoir as the sole evidence for a complete audit.

Validate uniformity on synthetic streams by checking inclusion frequency across early and late positions. Monitor seen count, sample size, partition balance, and duplicate IDs. A sample that is statistically correct but drawn after an upstream filter can still misrepresent the original population, so document the point in the pipeline where sampling occurs.

## Design review

Is the unit an event, user, or session? Does every unit get one unbiased chance? How are partition samples merged? Is the desired window cumulative or recent? Which downstream estimate needs inclusion probabilities or stratification weights?

10.11:
A t-digest is a compact, mergeable summary for estimating quantiles of numeric data. It is attractive for latency distributions because it aims for good accuracy near the tails, where p99 and p99.9 live. It does not store every observation, so a percentile is an estimate whose quality depends on compression settings, implementation, sample distribution, and merge order. For a small dataset or a high-stakes exact report, sort the raw values instead.

## Keep weighted centroids

A t-digest groups nearby values into centroids with a mean and weight. It keeps tighter groups near the extremes of the distribution and allows larger groups near the middle. New values are inserted or buffered and centroids are periodically compressed. To estimate a quantile, the digest walks cumulative weights and interpolates. The reference implementation by Ted Dunning documents online updates, merging, and tuning through a compression parameter.

The number of retained centroids is much smaller than the number of observations, which bounds memory in a stream processor. That saving comes with approximation. Two latency distributions can have similar median and very different p99; preserve enough tail detail for the alerting threshold. Test repeated identical values, long-tailed values, and sudden distribution shifts, because these are common in real latency data.

## Merge without averaging percentiles

Each service instance can build a t-digest for a time bucket and send it to an aggregator. The aggregator merges digests to estimate a fleet-wide percentile. Averaging instance p99 values is wrong: percentiles are not additive, and instances may have different request volumes. A digest merge carries weights and approximates the union distribution. All inputs need the same units, event definition, and compatible serialization. A digest of milliseconds and one of seconds can merge into nonsense while still producing a number.

Keep the bucket ID and input range with each digest. If a worker retransmits the same snapshot and the reducer merges it twice, the distribution becomes weighted twice. Use versioned replacement or deduplicate by partition and offset range. If a late event arrives after a bucket is published, merge a correction digest or republish the entire bucket with a higher version. State whether the report is provisional.

## Compare error where decisions happen

Benchmark the chosen implementation against exact sorted samples at p50, p95, p99, and p99.9 over representative traffic. Report both rank error and value error; a small rank difference can mean a large latency difference in a heavy tail. Apache DataSketches compares t-digest with KLL and emphasizes that their error profiles differ. Choose the sketch for the percentile and accuracy target, not because one name is familiar.

Monitor update throughput, digest size, merge time, input count, and discrepancies against exact sampled windows. A t-digest does not identify which request caused an outlier, so keep sampled traces or raw exemplars alongside the aggregate. Percentile alerts also need a minimum sample count; p99 of a handful of requests is unstable regardless of sketch quality.

## Design review

Which quantiles and units matter? What error at the tail is acceptable? Are digests merged with correct weights and without duplicate snapshots? How are late events handled? What exact sample validates the chosen compression and implementation?

10.12:
Streaming percentile analytics estimates the distribution of values as events arrive. It is often used for request latency, checkout duration, or delivery time. An average hides a long tail: 99 fast requests and one very slow request can have an acceptable mean while the slow user has a poor experience. A percentile answers a rank question, such as the value below which 99% of observations fall. The pipeline must preserve the distribution well enough for the chosen decisions.

## Define the measurement population

Choose the start and end of the measured operation, units, success and failure treatment, and grouping dimensions. A p99 over all API routes can be dominated by one high-volume fast route and hide a slow low-volume checkout route. Report by route or critical journey, but avoid exploding into millions of low-sample labels. Include sample count beside every percentile. A p99 from 20 observations is unstable because one observation determines much of the tail.

Choose event-time or processing-time windows and a late-data policy. A five-minute dashboard can be provisional until delayed events arrive. Beam's windowing model makes the watermark and trigger choices explicit. Keep a revision marker if published values can change. Do not average five-minute p99 values to produce an hour's p99; merge distribution summaries or recompute from raw values, weighted by observation count.

## Pick a summary and validate it

An exact percentile sorts all values in a bucket. That can be feasible for small or closed reports but costly for continuous high-cardinality monitoring. A histogram keeps counts in value buckets and can merge by adding corresponding bins; its error depends on bucket widths. A t-digest or KLL sketch keeps a compact approximate distribution and supports merges, with different accuracy profiles. Apache DataSketches documents KLL rank error and compares it with t-digest. Choose based on the required p99 value accuracy, not only memory usage.

Build local summaries per worker and time bucket, then merge compatible summaries in a reducer. Include units, sketch parameters, schema version, partition, and input range. Duplicate partial merges can alter a distribution; missing partitions can make it look healthier than reality. A highly skewed value such as a timeout cap should be represented consistently, not dropped from one service and included by another.

## Tie percentiles to action

Alerting on p99 requires a minimum volume and a threshold sustained across enough windows to avoid noise. Pair percentile with error rate and throughput: a sudden drop in p99 may mean slow requests are timing out or never reaching the measurement point. Keep exemplars or sampled traces for high-latency observations so engineers can investigate causes; a sketch cannot identify individual requests.

Compare stream estimates with exact calculations on sampled buckets, including repeated values and extreme tails. Monitor ingestion lag, window completeness, sketch merge errors, percentile drift, and per-label cardinality. A dashboard should state whether values are exact, approximate, or provisional. The number is useful only if its population and error are understood.

## Design review

Which requests enter the population? What sample count makes p99 meaningful? Can summaries merge across workers without duplicate input? What error at the alert threshold is tolerable? How will an outlier be traced after the sketch reports it?

10.13:
Live reactions let many viewers add or remove an emoji while a stream or post is active. A viral item can receive a burst of writes and fan the changing count out to far more watchers. Separate the authoritative reaction state from the low-latency display count. The user should get a clear result for their own action, while aggregate counts may be slightly delayed or coalesced.

## Define the reaction state transition

For a one-reaction-per-user rule, model a row or key `(item_id, user_id, reaction_type)` with an active state or use `(item_id, user_id)` if only one type is allowed at a time. A request has an idempotency key or a desired final state such as `set 👍` or `remove 👍`. A blind “increment” request retried after a timeout can add twice. Apply a conditional insert, delete, or state transition and emit an event only when the state actually changes. If anonymous reactions are permitted, define the weaker identity and abuse controls explicitly.

The authoritative store may be a partitioned database that enforces uniqueness. A single counter row for a viral item can be too hot, so aggregate accepted transitions through a stream into sharded counters or short time buckets. A user's reaction status should be read from their authoritative state; the public count can come from the derived aggregate. Reconcile the count from reaction rows or events when the aggregator falls behind or a bug is found.

## Broadcast at a controlled rate

Do not push a network message for every reaction to every viewer. At a million watchers, one thousand reactions per second could imply a billion outgoing messages per second. Coalesce counts on the server, for example publishing the latest total a few times each second, and let gateways fan out one update per interval to subscribed clients. A WebSocket or SSE connection can carry these updates. Include a monotonically increasing version or timestamp so a delayed update does not replace a newer count in the UI.

Partition subscriptions by item and gateway. A gateway keeps local connected viewers; a pub/sub layer sends each item update to gateways that have interested clients. Avoid broadcasting every item to every gateway. A slow client should receive the latest state rather than an unbounded backlog of obsolete intermediate totals. If a connection drops, the client fetches a fresh snapshot and resumes from there. The live count is a state, not a ledger of every intermediate display frame.

## Bound abuse and prove recovery

Rate limit reaction changes per user and item, validate item visibility, and prevent unauthorized clients from subscribing to private streams. A bot can still create many accounts, so monitor distinct actors, write bursts, and reversal patterns. Keep durable events for count recovery but only for a defined retention period. A queue outage can delay the public count while the accepted user state remains valid; show or log that lag rather than inventing a number.

Measure accepted transitions, duplicate requests, aggregation delay, broadcast fanout, gateway memory and connection count, dropped updates, reconnect snapshot rate, and drift between stored reactions and displayed counts. Load-test one extremely popular item because average traffic hides the key hot spot. The design succeeds when a user's own reaction is correct and the public display remains responsive without requiring per-reaction global broadcast.

## Design review

What unique state prevents duplicate reactions? Does an unlike reverse only a prior active reaction? How often is the aggregate broadcast, and to which gateways? Can a slow or reconnecting client recover the latest version? How is count drift reconciled?

11.01:
A realtime application keeps many clients informed when shared state changes. A WebSocket connection offers a bidirectional channel, but opening sockets is only the first problem. The system must authenticate and track subscriptions, route updates to the right gateways, recover after disconnects, and keep the database authoritative. A live screen should be a projection of durable state, not the only place where an update exists.

## Separate state from connections

Store accepted writes in an authoritative database with versions or sequence numbers. Publish a change event after the write commits, using an outbox or equivalent reliable path when loss matters. WebSocket gateways hold client connections and local subscription maps, but they should be replaceable. A gateway restart drops connections; clients reconnect, fetch a snapshot, and resume updates from a known version. Do not depend on an in-memory gateway map to preserve the only copy of an action.

RFC 6455 defines the WebSocket protocol and its bidirectional frames. The application still needs its own message contract: subscribe, unsubscribe, snapshot version, change event, acknowledgment, error, and heartbeat. Authenticate during connection setup and authorize each subscription, because a user may have access to one room but not another. Recheck or revoke authorization when membership changes; a long-lived connection does not make yesterday's permission permanent.

## Route updates to interested gateways

Partition events by document, room, or topic. A gateway subscribes to backend channels only for topics with local clients, then fans each update to those clients. Broadcasting every database change to every gateway wastes bandwidth. A large room may have clients across many gateways; coalesce rapid state updates or publish deltas under a bounded rate. Discord's engineering account of a million-user server illustrates the scale of one hot subscription and the need to control fanout.

Plan capacity from concurrent sockets, messages per second, bytes per message, and hot-topic fanout. A socket consumes memory, file descriptors, heartbeat traffic, and load-balancer state even when idle. Autoscaling gateways should account for connection draining and reconnection storms. Sticky routing can reduce resubscription work, but correctness should survive a client landing on another gateway.

## Handle gaps and slow clients

Attach a monotonically increasing version to each topic update. If a client sees version 105 after 103, it knows a gap may exist and can fetch a fresh snapshot or request replay from a retained log. Do not assume a WebSocket delivery is durable merely because a send call succeeded; the client may disconnect before applying it. A slow client should receive a bounded queue, a coalesced latest state, or a disconnect-and-resync instruction rather than exhaust gateway memory.

Measure active connections, subscriptions per gateway, publish-to-visible delay, dropped or coalesced messages, reconnect rate, snapshot fetch load, and version-gap repairs. Test database outage, broker outage, gateway restart, and a single room with extreme fanout. The system's promise should specify whether every intermediate event must be delivered or whether the latest correct state is sufficient.

## Design review

Which store owns the state? How does a client resume after a gap? Are subscriptions authorized for the whole connection lifetime? What happens when one room is much hotter than average? How is a slow client prevented from consuming unbounded memory?

11.02:
WebSockets, server-sent events (SSE), and long polling all deliver updates to a client, but they have different communication shapes. Choose from the traffic pattern and recovery contract. A dashboard that only receives status changes may fit SSE; a collaborative editor with frequent client and server messages may fit WebSockets; a constrained environment may need long polling. None of these transports automatically provides durable delivery or authorization.

## Compare the wire behavior

WebSocket begins with an HTTP handshake and then uses a bidirectional framed connection defined by RFC 6455. Both sides can send messages without a new HTTP request. SSE keeps an HTTP response open and streams text events from server to browser. The browser's `EventSource` API handles reconnection and can send the last event ID; client writes use ordinary HTTP requests. Long polling sends an HTTP request that the server holds until an update or timeout, then the client sends another. It works with familiar HTTP infrastructure but repeats request setup and can create a large number of held requests.

For all three, account for proxy timeouts, mobile networks, idle connections, load-balancer limits, and browser behavior. SSE is simple for one-way updates and uses standard HTTP response semantics, but browser connection limits can matter under some HTTP versions and deployment patterns. WebSockets have application-level ping/pong and require infrastructure configured for long-lived upgraded connections. Long polling often works through restrictive intermediaries, at the cost of more header traffic and repeated state coordination.

## Add a delivery protocol above transport

Give each update a topic and monotonic event ID or version. A client reconnects with its last applied ID, and the server either replays from a bounded log or instructs it to fetch a snapshot. SSE has a built-in `id` field and `Last-Event-ID` behavior described by MDN, but the server still decides whether that ID is authorized and replayable. For WebSockets, define the equivalent resume message. For long polling, include a cursor in each request and response.

Backpressure differs. A fast WebSocket producer can fill a slow client's outbound buffer; cap it and resync or disconnect. SSE writes can also block on slow clients, while long polling naturally limits outstanding responses but may accumulate server-held requests. Coalesce state updates when only the latest value matters. For a chat transcript where every message matters, retain the messages and use the transport only to notify clients that new durable records exist.

## Choose for the whole system

Estimate simultaneous clients, update rate, client write rate, average payload, and reconnect storms. SSE plus POST can be simpler than WebSockets when client writes are rare. WebSocket may reduce round trips when both sides send frequently. Long polling can be a compatibility fallback. Support one primary protocol well before adding multiple transports, because each adds reconnection and observability paths.

Measure time to first update, delivery lag, connection churn, missed-version repairs, bytes per client, and server resources per connection. Test suspend/resume on mobile, proxy idle timeout, authentication expiry, and server failover. The deciding question is what application state the client can reconstruct after interruption, not only which transport has the lowest idle overhead.

## Design review

Are updates one-way or bidirectional? How does a reconnect identify missed data? What is the behavior under a slow client? Which proxies and clients must be supported? Is the stream a notification of durable state or the sole record of events?

11.03:
A social network database stores users, relationships, posts, interactions, and visibility rules. The data model should support the main access patterns: fetch a profile, list whom a user follows, list followers, show a feed, and check whether one user may see a post. A graph label alone does not solve these queries. Most designs combine an authoritative transactional model for relationships and posts with derived indexes for feeds and recommendations.

## Model edges explicitly

A follow edge can be `(follower_id, followee_id, created_at, state)` with a unique constraint on the two IDs. Index by follower to list followed accounts and by followee to list followers. A private account may need `requested`, `accepted`, and `rejected` transitions rather than a single Boolean. Blocks and mutes have different effects: a block may revoke access, while a mute may only remove feed entries. Store them as distinct edge types or tables with documented precedence.

Follower counts can be derived, cached, or maintained transactionally depending on accuracy needs. A count should not be the sole record of relationships. Deleting an account or changing privacy must remove or hide edges in all read models. A cache of “who follows whom” needs invalidation or a versioned freshness bound, especially when used for access control.

## Keep post ownership and visibility clear

A post row needs a stable ID, author, creation time, content reference, visibility, moderation state, and version. Media belongs in object storage with metadata and permission checks. Edits and deletes should propagate to search and precomputed feeds. If a private post was copied into follower inboxes, each read must still enforce current visibility or remove stale entries promptly; fanout is a convenience index, not an authorization authority.

Use cursor pagination based on a stable ordering key such as `(created_at, post_id)` for large follower or post lists. Offset pagination becomes expensive and can skip or duplicate entries as new records arrive. For a feed, a ranking score may change, so a cursor needs a snapshot or clear best-effort semantics. Keep the authoritative post table separate from denormalized feed-entry references to avoid duplicating full content millions of times.

## Design for skew and change

Social graphs are highly skewed. An ordinary user may have 200 followers while a celebrity has millions. A write path that copies every post to every follower works for one and may overwhelm the system for the other. Choose push, pull, or hybrid feed generation based on measured follower distribution. Shard edge lists by owner or counterpart as queries demand, and plan how to count or page a very large list without loading it all into memory.

Monitor edge mutation latency, follower/following list latency, count drift, feed freshness, privacy-filter misses, and delete propagation. Test follow/unfollow races, block precedence, private-account approval, and a celebrity publish burst. Twitter's FlockDB project is an example of adjacency-list-oriented graph storage built for social edges, with an explicit focus on lookups rather than arbitrary graph traversals.

## Design review

Which relationship transitions exist? What indexes answer both edge directions? Which store enforces post visibility at read time? How do deletes reach feed and search projections? What breaks when an account has millions of edges?

11.04:
FlockDB was Twitter's distributed store for large social adjacency lists. Its public archive describes a specific workload: add and remove directed edges, list edges in either direction, page through huge lists, and perform some set operations. It was not built for arbitrary multi-hop graph traversal. That distinction is useful when designing a follow graph today: choose the data model for the queries the product actually runs.

## Store directed edges for both directions

A follow from A to B is not symmetric. The product needs “whom does A follow?” and “who follows B?” FlockDB stored a forward row keyed by source and a backward row keyed by destination, each with a sort position and state. The duplicate representation makes both lists efficient but adds write coordination and repair work. In a relational design, two indexes on an authoritative edge table can serve the same small-scale access patterns; at huge scale, separately partitioned read copies can avoid expensive cross-node scans.

Give each edge a stable identity and state such as active, removed, or archived. Follow and unfollow events may be retried or arrive out of order. A version or monotonic state transition prevents an old follow retry from reactivating a newer unfollow. FlockDB's notes explicitly mention tolerating duplicate and reordered operations. If forward and reverse projections differ temporarily, define which is authoritative and run reconciliation so counts and lists converge.

## Page lists without scanning from the start

A celebrity may have millions of followers. Offset pagination forces the database to skip ever more rows to reach a later page and can move under concurrent changes. FlockDB used a sort position as a cursor for indexed range scans. Pair the position with a unique edge ID to break ties, and define whether a client sees a stable snapshot or a changing live list. A follow that arrives while paging may appear on an earlier page and not be seen until refresh; that is a product behavior to document.

Set operations such as “people I follow who also follow B” can be built from indexed adjacency queries and intersections. Do not assume a general graph traversal engine is needed. Conversely, a product asking for recommendations across multiple hops, community detection, or path search may need a separate offline graph computation or a different store. The adjacency list answers one-hop queries very well; it does not make every graph algorithm cheap.

## Plan partitioning and recovery

Partition forward lists by source and reverse lists by destination. A hot celebrity's reverse list may still be large, so shard or bucket within that owner if a single partition cannot hold or serve it. Track edge mutation lag between directions, page latency, count drift, and repair backlog. Store durable mutation events so a failed reverse write can be retried and projections rebuilt. Privacy changes such as blocks should be checked at read time if eventual edge projection lag could expose content.

The FlockDB repository is archived and no longer maintained, so it is a design case study, not an automatic software recommendation. Its lasting lesson is to narrow the workload: an adjacency-list system can be simpler and faster than a general graph database when the main questions are one-hop lists and indexed set arithmetic.

## Design review

Which one-hop queries must be fast? Is the edge stored in both directions or served by two indexes? How are retries and out-of-order mutations resolved? Can a million-edge list be paged predictably? Which graph questions would require another system?

11.05:
Feed generation selects posts from accounts a user follows and orders them for display. The central tradeoff is when to do the distribution work. Push fanout writes a post reference into follower inboxes at publish time. Pull fanout reads recent posts from followed accounts when a user opens the feed. A hybrid uses both for different author sizes or freshness needs. The choice depends on follower skew, read frequency, ranking complexity, and acceptable delay.

## Compare push and pull costs

If an ordinary author has 200 followers, inserting 200 feed references may be cheap and make each follower's feed read fast. If a celebrity has ten million followers, one post can create ten million writes and a long queue. Pull avoids that publish burst by storing the post once, but a user following thousands of accounts may require many reads and a large merge on every feed open. The approximate load is not just total users; examine the distribution of followers and followed accounts, post rate, and feed-open rate.

A hybrid pushes ordinary authors and fetches high-follower authors on read. At read time, merge precomputed inbox entries with pulled posts, deduplicate by post ID, apply visibility checks, then rank and page. The threshold should be chosen from measured write and read costs, not a fixed folklore number. A celebrity might also have extremely active followers, so no single threshold works for every product.

## Keep the source and projection separate

Store the authoritative post once with author, timestamp, visibility, and version. An inbox entry contains a post ID and metadata for candidate retrieval. A fanout job must be restartable and idempotent with a unique `(viewer_id, post_id)` key. Record progress through follower pages so a crash does not require starting from zero. FlockDB's original design notes show why paging huge follower lists was an explicit requirement for tweet delivery.

Follow relationships can change while fanout runs. Decide whether a new follower receives older posts and whether an unfollow removes existing inbox entries. Regardless of denormalized entries, apply current blocks, privacy, and moderation state at read time. A deleted post must disappear even if stale references remain in inbox storage. Maintain a repair job that can reconstruct inbox entries from posts and relationships within a bounded history window.

## Rank and serve with a stable cursor

A chronological feed can page by timestamp and post ID. A ranked feed may mix freshness, relevance, and interactions, so scores can change between pages. Use a cursor tied to a ranking snapshot or accept documented best-effort pagination with possible movement. Fetch more candidates than the display page needs because deduplication and visibility filtering will remove some. Cache the first page for active users only when invalidation and privacy are correct.

Measure publish-to-visible lag by author class, fanout queue depth, feed-open p95 latency, missing-entry repair rate, and privacy-filter rejections. Test a celebrity publish burst and a user who follows thousands of accounts. The system should keep publishing responsive even when fanout is delayed, and the UI should not imply that every follower has received a post as soon as the author's write succeeds.

## Design review

What are the follower and followee count distributions? Which authors are pushed versus pulled? How does fanout resume after partial completion? Is visibility enforced at read time? How stable are pages when ranking and relationships change?

11.06:
A newly-unread indicator tells a user that content arrived after the point they last viewed. It can be a dot, a number, or a per-conversation badge. The design needs a precise boundary: “unread” may mean created since last open, delivered since last acknowledged, or not yet rendered. A dot often needs only a Boolean; an exact count needs more state and more updates.

## Use a cursor when the timeline is ordered

For a simple ordered inbox, store a per-user read cursor such as the highest seen message sequence. New items with a higher sequence make the indicator true. The client marks seen up to a chosen sequence only after it has displayed or acknowledged those items according to the product rule. A monotonically increasing server sequence is safer than client wall-clock time, which can be skewed. The update to the cursor should be monotonic so an old device cannot move it backward.

One global cursor does not cover every feed. Items may be filtered, deleted, or delivered out of order; a user can read a newer item but not an older one. For a conversation list, store per-conversation cursors or last-read IDs. For a feed, a “new posts since last visit” dot can compare the latest eligible post sequence with a visit watermark, while an exact count may require querying or maintaining a per-user unread set. State the product semantics before using the simplest cursor.

## Deliver a hint, then reconcile

A WebSocket or SSE event can tell an open client that a new item exists. The event is only a hint; after reconnect, the client should fetch current unread state from the authoritative service. Give updates a version so a delayed `unread = true` does not replace a later `unread = false` after the user opens the inbox. If a user reads on one device, publish the new cursor to other devices and let them refresh. A dropped live event should not permanently hide unread content.

The count may be cached or aggregated, but it must not become negative after concurrent read and arrival events. A transaction or compare-and-set can advance the read cursor and derive the count from item sequences. If maintaining a materialized count, reconcile it periodically against the underlying items and cursor. Redis Streams documents per-consumer cursors and ordered IDs, which illustrate the cursor idea, though a product's per-user read semantics still need their own model.

## Respect visibility and scale

Only eligible, visible items should trigger unread state. A blocked author's post, a deleted notification, or a message in a muted conversation may follow different rules. Recheck visibility when computing the badge, especially if fanout projections lag. Avoid sending every new item to every device as a separate badge update; coalesce high-rate changes and send the latest version. For a huge inbox, query by indexed sequence and user rather than scanning all historical entries.

Measure unread-state update lag, cross-device convergence time, cursor regression attempts, count drift, and reconnect snapshot rate. Test simultaneous reading on two devices, an item arriving during a read, deletion, and a long offline interval. A trustworthy dot is better than an “exact” number that is often wrong.

## Design review

What user action marks content read? Is unread a Boolean or an exact count? Which monotonic sequence defines newness? Can an old device regress the cursor? How does a reconnect repair missed live hints and stale cached counts?
