11.07:
Hashtags turn marked phrases in user content into navigable topics. The system must parse text consistently, store a relationship between post and tag, and serve recent or ranked posts for a tag. A simple `#\w+` regular expression is fragile across languages, combining marks, emoji, punctuation, and edited posts. Define the accepted syntax as a product contract and version the parser.

## Extract from displayed text

Parse the final stored text, not an untrusted client-provided list of tags. Normalize the tag key for matching while preserving the original display spelling. Unicode Standard Annex #31 discusses hashtag identifier boundaries, and UAX #29 describes word segmentation across scripts. Decide whether underscores, digits, emoji, and combining marks are allowed; test scripts without whitespace word boundaries. A tag should not begin in the middle of a longer identifier, and a URL fragment should not accidentally become a topic if the product excludes it.

Keep character offsets or source spans so the UI can link the exact hashtag without reparsing under a different rule. A post edit may add or remove tags. Re-extract with the current agreed parser version, calculate added and removed `(post_id, tag_key)` edges, and apply them idempotently. A parser upgrade may require reindexing old posts; keep the version so old and new results do not silently disagree.

## Model the tag relationship

Store a canonical tag row and a join table keyed by `(tag_key, post_id)` with post creation time, visibility metadata, and perhaps a ranking signal. Index by tag and time for a recent-post page. A unique constraint prevents a post repeating `#design` three times from appearing three times in the tag feed, unless the product explicitly wants occurrence counts. Keep the post as the source of truth for body text and access rules; the tag join is a derived index.

Hot tags can make one tag partition enormous during an event. Partition entries by time or bucket, use cursor pagination, and cache the first page with a short freshness bound. A trending count can be built from accepted tag events in time buckets, with spam filtering. Do not let raw mention volume alone define trend quality: bots can coordinate a burst. Retain an audit or replay path so tag indexes can be rebuilt after parser bugs.

## Serve safely and measure drift

Tag pages must filter deleted, private, blocked, and moderated posts at read time or remove them promptly from the projection. A stale join row should not reveal a private post. Normalize query tags with the same policy as stored tags, and redirect variants to one canonical URL only when they are truly equivalent. Case folding may be language-sensitive, so test representative locales rather than assuming ASCII lowercase is enough.

Measure extraction errors, tag-index lag, duplicate edge attempts, hot-tag query latency, moderation-filter rejections, and drift between tags parsed from posts and stored edges. Test edits, deletion, emoji and non-Latin text, and a sudden global trend. The goal is a stable, explainable topic link, not just a token that starts with `#`.

## Design review

What exact characters and boundaries form a tag? Is extraction server-owned and versioned? Can edits and retries update tag edges safely? How are hot tags paged? Can a stale tag index expose content that is no longer visible?

11.08:
Reaction modeling records who reacted to what and derives counts for display. A heart, thumbs-up, or emoji may look like a counter, but a user can retry, switch type, remove a reaction, or react from multiple devices. Model the user's desired state first and compute aggregates from accepted state changes. This makes idempotency and “unlike” behavior much easier to reason about.

## Choose the uniqueness rule

If a user may select only one reaction per item, use a unique key `(item_id, user_id)` and store `reaction_type`, state, and version. A new selection updates the existing row. If multiple types are allowed simultaneously, the unique key includes `reaction_type`. State the rule clearly; otherwise an API might accidentally allow five thumbs-up entries from one user. PostgreSQL unique constraints and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` provide one transactional way to enforce and update the state.

Prefer an API like `PUT /items/{id}/reaction` with the desired type or `DELETE` to remove it over a blind `toggle` when retries are possible. Sending the same desired state twice has the same outcome. If a toggle is required by the UI, attach an idempotency key and a known prior version so a retry does not reverse the action again. Return the authoritative user state and a count snapshot or version after the mutation.

## Derive counts from transitions

When a new reaction is inserted, increment its type count. When a reaction changes from 👍 to ❤️, decrement one and increment the other. When removed, decrement only if an active row existed. Emit a transition event after the state transaction commits, perhaps through an outbox. A duplicate event must not apply the count delta twice, so the aggregator tracks event IDs or computes counts from the current reaction table during reconciliation. The aggregate is a projection, not the authority for whether one user reacted.

For a viral item, updating one exact count row on every reaction may become a hotspot. Shard counters or aggregate events in small batches, accepting a short display lag. Keep a per-user state lookup fast and independent of the public count. A client can show its own reaction immediately after acknowledgment while the global count catches up. If the item is deleted or made private, block further reactions and hide the count according to visibility policy.

## Handle concurrency and abuse

Two devices can set different reaction types at nearly the same time. Decide whether last committed update wins or require a version check and conflict response. A monotonically increasing row version helps clients avoid applying an older response after a newer one. Rate limit rapid changes and monitor accounts that generate unnatural patterns. Avoid counting unauthenticated or bot activity as normal user engagement without a stated policy.

Measure accepted transitions, duplicate requests, count lag, drift between aggregate and reaction rows, and top-item write contention. Test insert, duplicate insert, switch, remove, retry after timeout, simultaneous devices, and recovery from aggregator failure. A design that keeps state transitions correct can always rebuild the display count; a design that only keeps a number cannot explain who owns a reaction.

## Design review

Can one user react once or once per type? Is the API a desired-state operation or a toggle? Which transition changes each count? Can replay apply a delta twice? How is a hot item's count scaled and reconciled?

11.09:
Photo tagging attaches a person, object, or label to a location within an image. The coordinate must survive thumbnails, responsive layouts, crops, rotations, and image replacement. Store tags in the image's own coordinate space, then transform them for each displayed rendition. Keep tag identity, permission, and moderation separate from the geometric point.

## Choose a canonical coordinate system

After applying image orientation, record the canonical image width and height and store a normalized point such as `(x / width, y / height)` in the range `[0,1]`. A rectangular tag can store normalized bounds. Normalized coordinates scale naturally to different display sizes. Validate bounds and reject NaN or infinite values. Keep the orientation and crop transform associated with the image version; a point from an old version may no longer identify the same face or object after replacement.

When the UI displays an image with `object-fit: contain`, the full image is visible with letterboxing; the pointer position must subtract that padding before normalizing. With `cover`, parts of the image are clipped, so the mapping must account for the scaled image and crop offset. MDN documents how `object-fit` and intrinsic image dimensions affect rendering. Do not simply divide the pointer's position by the outer element width and height, or tags will drift when aspect ratios differ.

For a thumbnail derived with an explicit crop, save the crop rectangle in canonical coordinates. The client can map canonical tag points through that transform and omit tags outside the visible crop. A rotated or mirrored rendition needs the corresponding orientation transform. Test on portrait, landscape, square, high-density, and deliberately cropped images; a single desktop screenshot will not reveal the geometry bugs.

## Model the tag lifecycle

A tag row can include `photo_id`, tag ID, target user or text label, normalized position, creator, state, and image version. A person tag may require the tagged person's approval before public display. Removal or hiding must propagate to cached renditions and search indexes. Authorization should check whether the viewer may see the photo and the tag, not assume that knowing a tag URL grants access. A unique rule may prevent duplicate tags for the same person in one image, depending on the product.

Do not infer identity automatically unless the product explicitly supports that behavior and has appropriate consent and accuracy controls. False person tags can be harmful. Preserve an audit trail for edits and reports, but limit retention of sensitive identity data. Treat embedded location metadata as separate from visual tag coordinates; exposing camera GPS data is not required to place a tag on an image.

## Serve and test at scale

Query tags by photo ID with a small index, fetch photo metadata and current visibility, then render coordinates client-side. For pages with many thumbnails, avoid an extra request per image by batching tag summaries. Cache only under the photo's permission and version constraints. Measure tag placement error across renditions, moderation queue age, removal propagation, and stale-version tags. A photo replacement should either migrate tags through a known transform or invalidate them for review.

## Design review

Are coordinates relative to the oriented original image or a viewport? How are contain, cover, crop, and rotation mapped? What happens after image replacement? Can a person approve or remove their tag? Are tag permissions checked along with photo permissions?

11.10:
Live commentary combines a durable message timeline with low-latency delivery to people watching the same event. The core challenge is keeping the timeline authoritative while sending updates to many connected clients. A live socket is a delivery path, not the storage layer: viewers who reconnect must still be able to fetch missed comments in the correct order.

## Accept and order messages

Each comment needs an event ID, author, room or event ID, body, server timestamp, and moderation state. A client-generated idempotency key prevents a timeout retry from creating a second comment. Assign a sequence number within the event or room if the UI needs a stable order; wall-clock timestamps from different clients can be skewed. If one room's write rate is too high for a single sequence allocator, partition by subroom or accept a best-effort order with a deterministic tie-breaker.

Persist the comment before broadcasting it. A transaction can insert the message and an outbox event together; a relay publishes after commit. This avoids a client seeing a comment that disappears after a database rollback, and it avoids losing an accepted comment if the broker is temporarily unavailable. Redis Streams or another retained log can also provide ordered IDs and cursor-based replay, subject to its persistence and retention configuration.

## Fan out without overwhelming viewers

Organize connected clients into event subscriptions. A gateway receives each new comment once and sends it to local viewers; a broker or partitioned stream routes it to the gateways that have subscribers. For a huge live event, naive global broadcast multiplies each comment by every connected viewer. Apply room partitioning, regional gateways, and bounded message rates. If the interface can batch comments or briefly coalesce updates, do so during bursts while preserving every durable message in the history.

Send a cursor or sequence with every update. On reconnect, the viewer supplies the last applied cursor and the server replays a bounded range or returns a fresh page with a reset cursor. If the client is too far behind, do not queue hours of stale socket data; give it the latest page and a clear resync point. Slow clients need a bounded buffer and a disconnect path rather than unbounded memory growth.

## Moderate and protect the room

Apply room membership and event visibility on both message submission and subscription. Rate limit per account and per room, detect repeated spam, and allow moderators to hide a comment without rewriting history invisibly. Separate pending moderation from visible messages if the event requires review. Deleted or hidden comments must stop appearing in cached pages and downstream search. A user joining late may see only a time-bounded history window, so define retention and cursor behavior together.

Measure accepted comments per second, write-to-visible delay, replay volume, broker lag, dropped socket updates, moderation queue age, and reconnect rate. Test one extremely popular event, a gateway restart, a broker outage, and a client reconnecting with a stale cursor. The system is correct when durable history remains complete, visible ordering is understandable, and temporary delivery failure can be repaired.

## Design review

What component assigns message order? Is the comment durable before it is broadcast? How does a viewer resume after disconnect? What is the per-room fanout ceiling? How are moderation changes applied to replayed and cached history?

12.01:
Nearby search finds objects within a distance of a point and returns the closest useful results. Examples include restaurants around a user, couriers near a pickup, and devices within a service radius. The design must get coordinate order, distance units, and Earth geometry right before optimizing the index. Latitude and longitude are not ordinary Cartesian meters.

## Filter candidates, then rank by distance

Store each point with an explicit coordinate reference system and index. A geospatial index narrows candidates by bounding boxes or cells; the final predicate computes actual distance. PostGIS recommends `ST_DWithin` for radius filtering because it can use a spatial index, while `ST_Distance` alone may scan every row. With `geography`, `ST_DWithin` takes meters and accounts for Earth's shape; with projected `geometry`, distance units come from the spatial reference. PostGIS also documents that point X is longitude and Y is latitude, a common source of swapped-coordinate errors.

A typical query first filters by service eligibility and an indexed radius, then orders a bounded result set by exact distance and possibly rating, availability, or ETA. “Nearest” and “best” are different ranks. A straight-line radius can be a candidate filter for a driving-distance result, but routes, bridges, and road closures require a routing service. Return distance to the client with its units and calculation basis.

## Handle boundaries and geography

Near the poles or across the antimeridian, a rectangular longitude/latitude box can wrap or distort. Use geography-aware operations or split the search region into safe boxes before applying the exact distance test. A radius query may cover several spatial index cells; cell indexing is a candidate generator and can include false positives. Exact filtering is required at the end. If locations are noisy, GPS accuracy should influence radius and ranking rather than pretending every point is exact.

Freshness is often more important than raw query speed. A driver's location may expire after a short TTL, while a restaurant coordinate is mostly static. Store observation time and accuracy, discard stale moving objects, and update their location independently from profile data. A nearby result from a courier last seen an hour ago is misleading even if the distance calculation is perfect.

## Scale read and update paths

For a moderate catalog, a database spatial index is straightforward and supports exact predicates. For high-rate moving objects, keep a hot location index partitioned by city, cell, or service region, with durable records elsewhere. Geospatial cells can route candidate queries to relevant partitions, but neighboring cell coverage must be complete around the radius. Cache popular center-and-radius queries only for stable datasets and include time/freshness in invalidation.

Measure candidate count, exact-distance computations, p95 latency, location age, coordinate validation failures, and result coverage at cell or city borders. Test longitude wraparound, zero radius, invalid coordinates, and sparse areas. The query should state what qualifies as “near,” how stale locations are treated, and what tie-breaker decides equal-distance results.

## Design review

What distance metric and units does the product promise? Which indexed filter narrows candidates? Are coordinates stored with a known CRS and in lon/lat order? How does the query handle stale or noisy moving points? Are cell or box candidates exact-filtered before display?

12.02:
Geohash encodes a latitude/longitude point as a string whose prefixes represent progressively smaller rectangular cells. The prefix property makes it convenient to store in a key-value or ordered index: objects sharing a prefix are geographically close at that resolution. But nearby points can land on opposite sides of a cell boundary, and rectangle dimensions vary by latitude. A prefix query is a candidate search, not a complete distance query.

## Use prefixes to narrow the search

The encoding repeatedly bisects longitude and latitude ranges, interleaves the decisions, and maps bits to characters. A short prefix covers a large rectangle; each additional character selects one of its child rectangles. Choose precision from the desired cell size and typical density. A city directory might use a coarser prefix than a doorstep delivery feature. Longer prefixes reduce candidates but increase the number of neighboring cells that must be searched around boundaries.

For a radius query, compute the query point's cell and the neighboring cells that intersect the radius. Fetch candidates from all relevant prefixes, then compute exact geodesic distance and filter. Searching only the query's prefix misses a café one meter away across a cell edge. Near the poles and antimeridian, coordinate wrapping makes neighbors especially important. Cell width shrinks with latitude while height is more stable, so “precision 7 means 150 meters” is not a universal guarantee.

## Store and route consistently

Store both the original coordinates and geohash. The coordinates support exact calculations and map display; the hash supports prefix lookup and coarse routing. Keep the hash precision/version with the index configuration. If a record's location changes, update its old and new prefix entries atomically or make the index rebuildable, otherwise it may appear in both places or neither. Partitioning by a short prefix can localize regional queries, but a dense downtown cell may become a hot partition.

For global nearest-neighbor requests, expand outward through cells until the candidates include enough results and a distance lower bound proves no unvisited cell can contain a closer point. A fixed “search 3x3 neighbors” is only correct for bounded query radii and chosen precision. For varying radius, enumerate all intersecting cells or use a spatial database index. After retrieval, exact distance, visibility, and availability filters still determine the answer.

A useful operational detail is to keep the query's chosen precision separate from its maximum radius. A larger search radius may require progressively coarser or more numerous cells; silently truncating the cell list creates geographic blind spots. Emit the cells searched and the exact-filter result count in traces so a miss can be reproduced.

## Measure the approximation boundary

Benchmark candidate-to-result ratio, number of cells queried, hot-prefix skew, and missed-neighbor rate against exact spatial queries. Test points at cell edges, across 180° longitude, near the poles, and in both dense and sparse regions. A geohash prefix is good for sharding, bounding boxes, and coarse scans; it is poor as a direct proof of exact distance or uniformly sized area. Use it where its simple string ordering fits the storage layer, then preserve the geometry semantics in the final filter.

## Design review

Which precision meets the density and radius needs? How are adjacent cells selected completely? How are changing locations removed from old prefixes? Can one dense prefix become hot? What exact distance calculation rejects false positives?

12.03:
H3, S2, and geohash map latitude/longitude into discrete cells. A cell ID supports partitioning, aggregation, joins, and approximate neighborhood lookup. These systems differ in cell shape, hierarchy, distortion, and boundary behavior. Pick one based on the operation: a grid can make city-level aggregation easy, but it does not replace an exact point-in-polygon or distance test.

## Geohash: simple prefixes and rectangles

Geohash repeatedly bisects latitude and longitude intervals and interleaves the bits into a base-32 string. Prefixes identify parent rectangular regions and are easy to index lexicographically. Neighbor lookup and cell width require care: cells are not square everywhere, nearby coordinates can have unrelated prefixes at a boundary, and longitude wraps at the dateline. Geohash works well for coarse prefix partitioning and common database key patterns, provided queries enumerate every intersecting cell and refine candidates exactly.

## H3: hierarchical hexagons

Uber's H3 indexes the sphere with mostly hexagonal cells plus twelve pentagons at each resolution. Each hexagon has seven finer child cells. This makes local neighborhood and aggregation operations convenient, especially when comparing neighboring areas or aggregating trips. H3's documentation distinguishes exact logical containment in its hierarchy from approximate geometric containment: a point in an H3 cell's geometric shape and a child cell's parent relation are not identical in every boundary case. Resolution is discrete; choose it for the analysis scale, not as an exact meter radius.

## S2: hierarchical spherical cells

S2 projects the sphere onto six cube faces and subdivides them with a hierarchical Hilbert curve. Its cell IDs cover a sphere-aware hierarchy, and an `S2RegionCoverer` approximates arbitrary regions with a union of cells. This is useful for covering a polygon or cap with a bounded number of index keys. The cover may include extra area, so exact geometry checks remain necessary. S2's cell hierarchy is not the same as a regular latitude/longitude grid.

## Select by query and operational fit

Use a grid for spatial joins and pre-aggregation when neighboring cell IDs are practical. Compare cell area variation, neighbor enumeration, hierarchy depth, polygon covering quality, language support, and library maturity. H3's hex layout can reduce directional artifacts in some neighborhood analyses, while S2's spherical hierarchy offers flexible region coverings. Geohash's prefix strings are convenient in simple key-value indexes. None guarantees that all nearby points share a prefix or cell.

Store canonical coordinates and the grid version alongside cell ID. If the resolution or library version changes, reindex explicitly. Query a covering cell set, gather candidates, then apply the exact distance, geometry, and visibility predicate. Test poles, antimeridian crossings, cells around pentagons, and points exactly on boundaries. Compare candidate volume against true matches for real density distributions before committing to a grid.

The same location may be encoded at several resolutions for different consumers. A dispatch service can need fine cells while a city analytics job uses coarse cells. Keep these identifiers as separate derived fields; do not overwrite the canonical point with whichever grid the current query happens to use.

## Design review

Is the main operation neighborhood lookup, aggregation, or polygon covering? Which cell hierarchy and shape fit it? What boundary or distortion error is acceptable? Are exact predicates applied after cell retrieval? How will changes in resolution or grid version be migrated?

12.04:
Redis GEO can provide a fast in-memory path for nearby lookup when the working set and query shape fit one Redis deployment. It stores members with longitude and latitude and can search a circle or box. Treat it as a hot candidate index: validate coordinates, filter candidates, and preserve an authoritative source for location state and rebuilds. A Redis hit is not automatically the nearest eligible result after business and permission rules.

## Model the hot location set

Use a key per region or entity type, such as `drivers:city-7`, and add members with stable IDs and coordinates. Set a TTL or remove members when a moving object's location expires. Keep the observation timestamp outside the GEO score if freshness matters; Redis GEO commands represent location, not the business validity window. A driver last seen thirty minutes ago should not be offered merely because the stored point is nearby.

`GEOSEARCH` supports radius or box queries and can return distance or coordinates. Use `COUNT` to cap a broad candidate set only when the product can tolerate that bound. If you request too few nearby members before checking eligibility, stale, offline, or unavailable drivers may consume all returned slots and hide valid candidates just beyond them. Over-fetch adaptively or use an authoritative prefilter where possible.

## Keep writes and reads consistent enough

Location updates are frequent and often last-write-wins. Attach a source timestamp or sequence and reject older updates that arrive late. If a member changes city or region key, remove it from the old key and add it to the new one; an atomic script can update both when both keys share one Redis shard. If Redis Cluster key placement prevents that, make the durable location table authoritative and run reconciliation for duplicate or missing members.

Partition by city or service area to keep queries local, but support boundary searches that span keys. A query near the edge of a city region must inspect adjacent regions or use overlapping coverage. Cache a user's location for a short time only with consent and privacy controls. Redis persistence, replication, and eviction policy determine whether this hot index survives restart; plan for reload from the authoritative location feed.

## Measure candidate quality and resource use

Track query latency, result count before and after eligibility filters, member age, location update rate, key memory, eviction, and Redis hot-key pressure. Test dense downtown queries, sparse rural queries, antimeridian behavior, and a burst of location updates. Compare the chosen Redis GEO result set with an exact spatial reference sample. If radius semantics, complex polygon filters, or durable history dominate the workload, keep Redis for the hottest path and use a spatial database for broader queries.

Include cardinality limits in load tests: one city key that grows without bounds can consume memory and slow maintenance even when query times look good. Rebuild keys with an explicit cutover if the member schema or partition boundaries change.

## Design review

Which records belong in the hot set, and how long are they valid? Can one Redis key become too hot? What happens when a query crosses region boundaries? How many candidates survive eligibility filters? How is the hot set rebuilt after eviction or restart?

12.05:
A geofence is a geographic region associated with an action: notify when a device enters a campus, restrict a delivery zone, or alert when equipment leaves a service area. The business question is often point-in-polygon, but the system must also handle location noise, boundary policy, changing polygons, and repeated GPS updates. A correct geometry test by itself does not determine when a user should receive one notification.

## Store polygons with explicit semantics

Represent each zone as a polygon or multipolygon with a coordinate reference system, version, and active time range. Validate rings, self-intersections, holes, and orientation at ingestion. Decide whether a point on the boundary is inside. PostGIS `ST_Contains` excludes a point lying only on a polygon boundary, while `ST_Covers` includes boundary points. Either may fit, but different services must not silently use different rules.

For a single point check, a spatial database can use an index-aware predicate such as `ST_Covers(zone.geom, point)`. For many devices and a few zones, index zones and query candidates. For many zones and a device stream, use a spatial index or cell covering to find candidate zones, then perform exact point-in-polygon on each candidate. Bounding boxes and geohashes only prune; they do not prove containment.

## Convert noisy fixes into transitions

GPS points jitter around a boundary. If every fix triggers a notification, a user parked near the edge receives repeated enter and exit messages. Keep per-device, per-zone state and require a transition rule such as two consecutive fixes inside, a minimum dwell time, or a confidence radius contained within the zone. Use hysteresis: an entry threshold slightly inside and an exit threshold slightly outside can prevent rapid toggling. Do not apply these rules when a hard legal boundary requires immediate precise evaluation; clarify the accuracy requirement.

Assign each fix an observation time and source sequence. Ignore older fixes and expire device state after a chosen silence period. A location estimate has an uncertainty radius; if the uncertainty overlaps the boundary, report an indeterminate state or wait for a better fix rather than claiming precise entry. The product can distinguish “near the zone” from “inside.”

## Make notifications idempotent and auditable

Create a transition ID from device, zone, transition type, and state version. Queue notification work after state is durably updated. A retry should not send another alert for the same transition. When a zone changes, decide whether to re-evaluate every current device or apply the new boundary only to future fixes. Version zone geometry so a transition can be explained with the polygon that was active at the time.

Measure candidate zones per fix, geometry-test latency, GPS fix age, boundary uncertainty, duplicate transition rate, and notification delay. Test holes, multipolygons, boundary points, coordinate order, and GPS jitter. Keep location retention and access limited to the geofence purpose; a zone detector should not become an indefinite movement history by accident.

## Design review

Does the boundary count as inside? How are malformed polygons rejected? Which candidate index finds zones efficiently? What rule prevents GPS jitter from generating repeated transitions? Can a queued alert be explained and deduplicated?

12.06:
Ray casting is a classic point-in-polygon test. Cast a ray from the query point in a fixed direction and count how many polygon edges it crosses: an odd count means inside and an even count means outside. The idea is simple and works well for many planar polygons, but an implementation needs deliberate rules for vertices, horizontal edges, boundaries, holes, and floating-point precision.

## Apply the crossing test

For each edge from `(x1,y1)` to `(x2,y2)`, first check whether the edge straddles the horizontal ray's y-coordinate: one endpoint is at or below `y`, the other above. If so, compute the x-coordinate where the segment crosses that horizontal line. Toggle the inside flag when the intersection lies to the right of the point. Half-open comparisons avoid counting a polygon vertex twice when two adjacent edges meet exactly on the ray.

Do not divide by `(y2-y1)` for a horizontal edge without checking the straddle condition; horizontal edges do not cross a horizontal ray under the half-open rule. A point exactly on an edge or vertex needs a separate boundary test if the product requires a deterministic inside/outside answer. Franklin's PNPOLY notes explain a compact crossing implementation and its careful handling of edge cases. For a production GIS operation, a robust library is usually safer than copying a small snippet without its assumptions.

## Respect polygon structure

A simple ring can use parity directly. A polygon with holes uses even-odd parity across all rings, provided the rings are valid and the intended fill rule is defined. Multipolygons test each component. Self-intersecting rings may have ambiguous interior semantics and should be rejected or repaired by a geometry library at ingestion. Coordinate systems matter: longitude/latitude is not a flat uniform plane over the entire globe. Project small local regions to a suitable planar CRS or use a spherical geometry implementation for broad geography.

Before ray casting, use a bounding box or spatial index to avoid scanning every polygon edge for every point. A large polygon can have thousands of edges; edge indexing or prepared geometry speeds repeated tests. The bounding box is only a necessary condition, then the exact point-in-polygon predicate decides.

## Test degeneracies explicitly

Create test cases for a point well inside, outside, on an edge, on each vertex orientation, aligned with a horizontal edge, inside a hole, and near the antimeridian if geographic. Use integer or robust orientation predicates where practical. Floating-point rounding can change whether an intersection lies just left or right of a boundary. Compare your implementation with PostGIS or another geometry library on generated random polygons and boundary-focused tests.

Document the boundary rule in the API. If a geofence treats boundary points as inside, select a predicate such as `ST_Covers`; if it follows OGC `Contains` semantics, boundary-only points are excluded. The ray algorithm is a building block, not a license to leave semantics implicit.

## Design review

How are vertex intersections counted once? What is the boundary policy? Are holes and multipolygons supported? Is the chosen coordinate system planar enough? What robust library or reference implementation validates the result?

12.07:
A seen filter helps a service avoid returning an item a user has already viewed, received, or acted on. An exact set answers membership correctly but can be large. A Bloom filter stores a compact bit array and several hashes: it can say “definitely not seen” or “possibly seen.” It has false positives but no false negatives under its standard add-only model. That means it may hide a new item, so it is appropriate only when that error is acceptable.

## Size the filter for expected load

The false-positive probability depends on bit-array size, number of inserted elements, and number of hash functions. Configure for the expected capacity and error target. If a filter fills beyond its design capacity, false positives rise and a service may start hiding many unseen posts. Redis documents both capacity and false-positive configuration for Bloom filters. Monitor estimated insertions and observed false-positive rate; rotate or expand filters before they become saturated.

Use a stable item identity such as post ID plus feed version. If one user's “seen” state is stored in one filter, a global filter shared by all users produces incorrect results. Partition by user or by a bounded cohort, and include scope and time window in the key. A daily filter can expire after a week if the product only suppresses recent items. This keeps memory bounded and avoids an unbounded all-time history.

## Place false positives in the right stage

A Bloom filter is useful to skip a database membership lookup for items likely already seen. If it says “possibly present,” confirm against an exact store before suppressing the candidate. This preserves correctness while reducing most lookups. If the product accepts occasional omission, it can suppress directly, but expose that approximation in the design. A Bloom filter cannot enumerate seen IDs or remove one arbitrary ID; deletion needs a counting Bloom filter, a rotating generation, or exact state.

Filters used across a distributed pipeline need consistent updates. If writes are asynchronous, a newly seen item may still be returned until the filter catches up. If each region has a separate filter, users moving between regions may see duplicates. Use an event stream or exact durable table as the source and rebuild compact filters from it. Ensure filters are not used for authorization: a false positive or stale filter could deny valid access, and a false negative could reveal an item if the filter were treated as a permission gate.

## Compare with exact state

An exact set is necessary when every item must be accounted for, such as financial deduplication or strict “one impression ever” rules. A Bloom filter fits high-volume recommendation or feed suppression where one missed candidate has low cost. Hybrid designs use the filter for cheap negative checks and an exact database for positives. Test a saturated filter, duplicate additions, restart, and regional resync. Measure memory per user, false positives, exact lookup rate, and duplicate or missing item rate.

## Design review

What does “seen” mean and for how long? Are false positives allowed to hide a candidate? How is capacity chosen and saturation detected? Can an item be removed? Is the filter merely an optimization, or does it accidentally control access?

12.08:
Matching and recommendation systems select candidates that fit a user, context, or query, then rank a manageable subset. “Best match” can mean nearest by geography, similar by content, likely to be clicked, or compatible with hard constraints. Define the objective before choosing the algorithm. A recommender that ignores availability, safety, or diversity can optimize a metric while producing an unusable list.

## Separate candidate generation from ranking

Candidate generation searches a large catalog using one or several inexpensive methods: category filters, collaborative item similarity, user history, geographic proximity, or vector retrieval. A scoring stage estimates relevance for hundreds of candidates. A reranker then applies constraints and diversity to the top results. Google’s recommendation-system documentation describes this multi-stage pattern and why a small candidate set is needed for low-latency ranking. If the candidate generator misses an item, the ranker cannot recover it.

For collaborative filtering, implicit actions such as clicks or purchases are not explicit ratings. A click depends on exposure and rank, and no click may mean “not shown,” not “disliked.” Use positive and negative evidence carefully, normalize popularity, and preserve a fallback for new users and items with little interaction history. Content features and editorial or rule-based candidates help with cold start.

## Define features and freshness

A candidate score may combine user-item affinity, freshness, distance, quality, inventory, and context. Hard constraints should filter candidates, not merely contribute a small negative score. Model features need timestamps and versions: a location estimate from an hour ago or an out-of-stock cache can make a high score meaningless. Precompute stable item embeddings or neighbors, then apply fast user context at request time. Keep feature logs sufficient to explain why a result appeared.

Recommendations have feedback loops. Popular items receive more exposure and then more clicks, which can make them even more popular. Use exploration or diversity constraints where appropriate, and monitor concentration across creators or categories. A/B tests measure outcomes, but offline ranking metrics and guardrails for latency, safety, and coverage help identify regressions before rollout.

## Make the ranking useful under failure

Bound candidate count and per-stage deadlines. If personalization times out, serve a safe popularity or category fallback rather than an error page. Deduplicate candidates from several generators and avoid showing near-identical items together. Apply seen filtering with an explicit false-positive policy; one missed recommendation may be acceptable, while suppressing a transaction-required item may not be. Cache only when the cache key captures relevant user, region, and inventory context.

Measure candidate recall, ranking quality, coverage for new items, diversity, latency by stage, stale-feature rate, and fairness across relevant cohorts. Keep a small evaluation set for cold-start, sparse-history, and unusual-context users. Record ranking model version and feature snapshot so a recommendation can be reproduced later.

When a user reports an obviously wrong result, capture the candidate sources and filter decisions as well as the final score. That trace separates missing-candidate bugs from ranking mistakes.

## Design review

What is the objective and what are hard constraints? Which generators create candidates and how is recall measured? How does the system handle new users and items? Can feedback loops collapse diversity? What fallback is served when a model or feature store is slow?

# Direct-to-object-storage upload

Direct uploads let a client send large bytes to object storage without making an application server proxy every byte. The application still owns authorization, object identity, policy, and the transition from an untrusted upload to a usable asset. A safe flow is: client asks for an upload, API authenticates and checks quota, API creates an opaque upload record and a short-lived signed request for one staging key, client uploads, then client reports completion and the backend verifies the stored object before publishing it.

## Keep control and data planes separate

The API should return a generated object key, allowed method, required headers, expiry, and constraints such as maximum size and accepted content type. Do not let the client choose an arbitrary bucket key: an attacker could overwrite another user's object or place content in a public path. Scope the credential to one key and one operation. A presigned URL is a bearer capability: anyone who obtains it can use it until expiry, within the signer's permissions. Store it only in memory, avoid logging query strings, and use a short lifetime appropriate to expected upload duration. AWS documents that a presigned URL can be reused until expiration and that writing the same key replaces that object, so unique keys and one-time application state matter.

The browser sends bytes directly to storage. Configure CORS narrowly for the app origins and required methods and headers; CORS is a browser rule, not authorization. The API remains the authority for who may create an upload and whether it can become visible. For small files a single PUT is simple. For large or unreliable transfers, multipart upload allows independent parts and retries; the application needs an upload identifier, part numbers, and completion or abort semantics.

## Verify before accepting

A successful HTTP response proves storage accepted bytes, not that the object is safe or valid. On completion, the backend should `HEAD` the exact key, compare expected and observed size, record an ETag only as a storage-specific validator rather than assuming it is always a content MD5, and enqueue malware scanning or media inspection. Verify ownership against the upload record. Content type supplied by a browser is untrusted; detect type from bytes and apply format-specific parsers with resource limits. Keep staged objects private until processing succeeds. A state machine such as `created → uploading → received → scanning → ready` makes duplicate callbacks and retries manageable.

## Failures and cleanup

Clients can close the tab after storage succeeds but before notifying the API. A reconciler can find old upload records and inspect their keys. Conversely, a completion request can race a retry; make completion idempotent by persisting the verified object version and returning the same result. Delete abandoned staging objects after a retention window. For multipart uploads, explicitly abort failed sessions or configure storage lifecycle cleanup for incomplete parts, which otherwise consume space. Make retry policy bounded, with jitter, and avoid issuing a new key for every retry unless the old object is also cleaned up.

Track issued upload intents, successful bytes, failed requests by status, completion lag, abandoned bytes, scan rejection rate, and quota denials. Alert on growing staging age and storage errors. Test expired signatures, overwritten keys, forged completion events, oversized files, CORS preflight, and duplicate completion. The design should make the boundary obvious: a URL grants temporary byte-write access; it does not grant permission to publish the resulting asset.

## Design review

Does each signed request target one generated key and one operation? What limits size, type, and user quota? How does the server confirm bytes landed before accepting completion? Are staged objects private pending scanning? How are abandoned multipart parts and duplicate callbacks handled?

# Image CDN and resizing

An image delivery service turns an original upload into cacheable renditions suited to a device and placement. The central choice is whether transformations happen eagerly at ingest or lazily on demand. Eager generation makes serving predictable and avoids first-view work, but can produce many unused variants. Lazy resizing saves work for long-tail sizes, but needs abuse limits, cache design, and a strategy for cold transformations. Most systems combine a small standard rendition set with bounded on-demand variants.

## Define a canonical rendition identity

Represent a rendition as a deterministic tuple: source asset version, width, height or fit mode, output format, quality policy, and any crop parameters. Resolve that tuple to a canonical URL or internal cache key. A content version in the path makes updates safe: `/asset/abc/v7/w640/cover.webp` can have a long immutable cache lifetime, while a mutable alias needs revalidation or purge. Validate requested dimensions against a policy rather than allowing arbitrary width and height. Otherwise a client can request millions of distinct variants and turn the image service into an unbounded compute and cache workload.

The edge can serve an existing rendition or route a cache miss to a transformation service. That worker fetches the private original, decodes it with limits, transforms, writes an immutable result, and returns it. Keep the origin protected from direct public listing and use service credentials for the transform path. Normalize equivalent requests before caching: `?w=640&h=480` and reordered query parameters should not accidentally create separate objects. If format negotiation depends on `Accept`, include only a normalized supported format in the cache key or emit stable format-specific URLs. CloudFront's cache key documentation emphasizes that each additional header, cookie, or query variation can create another cache object; include only values that change the response.

## Protect decoders and control cost

Image parsers process attacker-controlled binary input. Apply byte-size, pixel-count, frame-count, CPU, and wall-time limits; reject malformed or decompression-bomb inputs. Decode in isolated workers with bounded memory. Strip EXIF metadata by default to reduce privacy leakage and avoid orientation inconsistencies. Preserve color profiles deliberately, and define how animated formats are handled. A thumbnail path should not silently decode a huge animation into memory. Validate that output dimensions and format match the canonical request before writing it.

On a miss, concurrent requests for the same rendition can stampede. Use a single-flight lock or idempotent conditional object creation keyed by the rendition identity. Locks need expiry and recovery if a worker dies. The CDN can coalesce some misses but should not be your only coordination guarantee. Set cache TTLs based on immutability: content-addressed or versioned paths can be cached for a long time; mutable endpoints should have short TTLs and a reliable invalidation plan. Purging every edge on every edit is expensive, so immutable versioned URLs are often simpler.

Measure hit ratio, transformation latency, queue depth, decode failures, origin bytes, rendition cardinality, and cost per source asset. Test odd aspect ratios, transparent images, animated files, extreme dimensions, query normalization, stale source versions, and simultaneous cold requests. The product contract should state crop behavior and whether a requested size is exact or a maximum box; that decision affects both UX and cache identity.

## Design review

Can every rendition be represented by a bounded, canonical key? Are originals private and immutable versions addressable? What limits defend image decoders? Which inputs change the CDN cache key? How do format negotiation, invalidation, and cold-miss stampedes behave?

# An avatar service

An avatar looks like a small image field, but it combines identity, upload, moderation, variant delivery, and cache invalidation. A useful design treats an avatar as a versioned asset attached to a user, rather than as bytes embedded in a profile row. The profile stores an asset identifier or immutable URL. The upload service owns bytes and processing; the profile service owns which accepted asset is currently selected.

## Separate asset creation from selection

The user first requests an upload intent. The server checks authentication, account status, and any product policy, then creates a private staging asset with an unpredictable identifier. The browser uploads directly to object storage using a short-lived scoped URL. A worker checks actual file type and dimensions, applies pixel and byte limits, strips metadata, scans or moderates content, and creates standardized square renditions. Until the asset is approved and fully processed, the profile continues pointing at the previous avatar. This avoids a blank avatar or unsafe upload becoming immediately visible.

When processing succeeds, a profile update atomically changes the selected avatar reference and increments an avatar version. If two browser tabs finish out of order, use a compare-and-set against an expected profile version or an explicit “latest user choice” token so a stale upload cannot unexpectedly replace a newer selection. Keep the asset lifecycle separate: an upload may be ready but not selected, and a selected asset may be replaced while the old object remains briefly for cache and rollback needs. Reference counting or delayed garbage collection is safer than deleting bytes inline with the profile update.

## Make delivery predictable

Serve a small set of rendition sizes through stable versioned URLs: for example, tiny list avatars, medium profile images, and a larger detail view. Include the avatar version in the path so the CDN can cache immutable objects aggressively. A mutable `/users/123/avatar` endpoint can redirect to that path, but it needs a short TTL or revalidation. Do not use a user-specific cookie or authorization token in a public avatar cache key unless the response truly varies by it; that fragments cache and can expose private variants if cache policy is incorrect. For private communities, issue signed delivery URLs or perform an authorization check before redirecting to a cacheable protected object.

Default avatars should be generated from a deterministic user seed or selected from a small shared catalog, not materialized as one unique image per account. A generic default has excellent cache reuse. The API should return an explicit fallback state so clients don't retry a missing image indefinitely. Include deletion and account closure semantics: remove the profile reference first, then schedule asset cleanup according to retention and legal requirements.

## Moderation, privacy, and resilience

Avatar processing is a user-generated-content pipeline. Make moderation decisions auditable, allow safe retry of transient scanning failures, and distinguish rejection from processing outage. Keep original uploads private and limit worker permissions to their required buckets. If the transform system is unavailable, keep the previous avatar and retry asynchronously. Rate-limit upload intents and cap pending assets per user to stop resource abuse. Avoid embedding sensitive identifiers in public object paths; opaque identifiers reduce casual enumeration but are not a substitute for access control.

Operationally monitor upload completion, processing age, moderation queue age, failed transforms, cache hit rate, stale-avatar reports, and garbage-collection lag. Test out-of-order uploads, rejected content, storage success with lost client callback, user deletion during processing, and CDN caching across avatar versions. A good avatar system preserves the last known-good image until its replacement has crossed the full validation boundary.

## Design review

Does the profile point only to a ready asset? How do competing uploads resolve? Are renditions versioned and safe to cache? What moderation and file limits apply? How does deletion interact with CDN TTLs and delayed cleanup?

# Video upload: signed URLs and multipart

Video uploads are large enough that the API should coordinate the transfer, while object storage receives the media bytes. A robust flow starts with an upload session: authenticate the user, check plan quota and expected size, reserve an opaque staging key, and return either a scoped single PUT URL or multipart instructions. Store the session state server-side so a client cannot complete an upload belonging to another account or publish an arbitrary storage key.

## Choose single-part or multipart

A single signed PUT is easy to reason about, but a failed transfer may require sending the entire file again. Multipart upload divides the object into numbered parts that can be sent concurrently and retried independently. The backend initiates the multipart operation and retains its storage upload ID. It can then issue short-lived part URLs in batches, or validate part requests through an upload gateway. The client reports each part's number, ETag, and checksum. The backend validates that every part belongs to the session and that the total is within policy before asking storage to complete the object. S3 assembles parts in ascending part-number order; its ETag for the combined object is not necessarily an MD5 of the full file. Use explicit checksums when integrity verification is needed.

Part size is a tradeoff: small parts increase request overhead and metadata; large parts waste more bandwidth when retried. Concurrency should be tuned to the client network and constrained so many simultaneous users do not overload storage request quotas or their own connection. Provide resumability by persisting the session identifier and completed parts, but make resume authorization expire and bind to the authenticated user. A refreshed client should query server-side parts rather than trusting a local list that may be stale.

## Complete through a state machine

Completion should be idempotent. A client may time out after storage completed the object and retry; the API should return the same accepted asset rather than create a second one. Model states such as `initiated`, `uploading`, `completing`, `received`, `validating`, `ready`, `rejected`, and `aborted`. Use a conditional state transition or transaction to prevent two completion calls racing. After completion, inspect the actual object size and metadata, verify checksums where supported, and run media probing before enqueueing transcoding. Do not trust client MIME type, filename, declared duration, or reported dimensions.

Incomplete multipart sessions retain uploaded parts and can incur storage charges. Abort on user cancellation or terminal errors, and configure lifecycle cleanup as a backstop. If part uploads are still in flight when abort starts, reconcile afterward because a late part may succeed. Keep originals private, use unique keys, and make the staging bucket inaccessible to playback clients. The signed URL is a limited bearer credential: avoid access logs that expose it, keep expiry reasonable, and scope it to expected headers and one upload session.

Monitor upload completion percentage, bytes, part retry rate, session age, abandoned storage, checksum failures, and time from completion to playback-ready. Test network loss mid-part, expiry during upload, repeated completion, part replacement, oversize objects, and stale resume state. The user-visible promise should clarify that transfer completion and playable video availability are separate milestones.

## Design review

When does a file use multipart? Who owns the multipart ID and completion list? Are checksums verified independently of ETags? Can completion be safely retried? How are orphaned parts cleaned up, and what does the client see while transcoding is pending?

# Video transcoding pipeline

Transcoding converts one uploaded source into renditions that fit supported codecs, resolutions, bitrates, and playback protocols. It is an asynchronous workload with expensive CPU or accelerator use, so the design should separate durable job intent from worker execution. Once upload validation succeeds, persist a media record and enqueue a job keyed by media ID and source version. Workers fetch the private source, probe streams, generate outputs, validate artifacts, and publish a manifest only after all required renditions are available.

## Make processing reproducible

Store the source object version or immutable key, detected codecs, duration, dimensions, audio tracks, and a versioned encoding profile. A profile defines codec settings, target ladder, segment format and duration, audio treatment, and output protocol. Pinning profile versions makes a retry reproducible and allows a deliberate re-encode later. The queue message should carry identifiers, not large metadata or signed URLs that expire before a delayed job runs. The worker obtains fresh credentials through a service identity and checks that the source version still matches the job.

Each output should have a deterministic path incorporating source revision and profile version. Write to a temporary namespace first; verify that segments and manifests exist, are decodable, have aligned timelines, and match expected dimensions and durations. Then atomically update the media record to a ready manifest pointer. This prevents a player from seeing half a package. If transcoding fails after some outputs were written, retries can reuse valid immutable outputs or delete them using a bounded cleanup process. Job execution is usually at least once, so workers must be idempotent.

## Control expensive work and noisy media

Probe before allocating a large transcode. Reject unreasonable duration, pixel count, stream count, malformed containers, or decompression behavior according to product policy. Run decoders in isolated workers with CPU, memory, disk, and wall-clock limits. Capacity planning uses source duration and codec complexity, not merely number of jobs; a ten-minute high-resolution source can consume far more compute than a short clip. Use separate queues or priorities for user-facing short clips and bulk reprocessing. Apply admission control when backlog exceeds a latency or budget threshold rather than accepting unlimited work.

A scheduler may split independent renditions across workers, but packaging requires consistent timestamps, keyframe boundaries, and shared audio/video timing. If the pipeline parallelizes, define a barrier that publishes only when all required tasks have completed. Optional renditions can be marked unavailable without blocking playback if the product tolerates fallback to a base rendition. Record the exact toolchain and profile version in job metadata for debugging and compliance.

Track queue wait, processing time per media minute, cost per output minute, worker failures by stage, retry count, invalid source ratio, ready latency, and orphaned bytes. Test corrupt containers, missing audio, variable frame rates, very long videos, worker loss, duplicate queue delivery, and a profile rollout. A dead-letter queue needs an operator path for replay after fixing the cause; simply retrying poison input forever hides failures and burns capacity.

## Design review

Is the input validated before expensive work? Can a retried job overwrite a published package? Are profile and source versions explicit? How is readiness committed atomically? What limits prevent a malformed video from monopolizing a worker pool?

# Adaptive bitrate and the CDN decider

Adaptive bitrate playback packages a title into several quality representations and lets the player choose which segment to fetch next. A manifest describes available renditions and where their segments live. The player estimates throughput, buffer health, decode capability, and sometimes viewport size, then selects a representation. This moves adaptation to the edge closest to user experience: the player sees local stalls and device constraints that a server cannot directly observe.

## Build an aligned rendition ladder

Encode several resolutions and bitrates, but avoid making every rung a separate unrelated video. Align segment boundaries and keyframes so a player can switch representations without visible gaps or timestamp discontinuities. The ladder should reflect source quality and likely device/network classes; upscaling a low-resolution source wastes bytes. Audio may be a shared rendition or paired tracks depending on language and packaging. Package HLS or MPEG-DASH manifests and segments as ordinary HTTP objects, which makes a CDN a natural delivery layer. Browser support and player choice influence whether one protocol or both are needed.

The player's decision can use an estimated bandwidth safety margin rather than chasing every short-lived throughput spike. A rule such as “choose a bitrate below a conservative fraction of recent goodput, unless buffer is critically low” trades sharpness for fewer stalls. Startup often favors a conservative representation to begin quickly; later choices can rise as the buffer grows. A player should avoid switching too often because oscillation is distracting, and should reduce quality promptly when buffer drains. Device decode limits and data-saving preferences can impose a cap even when bandwidth is ample.

## What the CDN decides

The CDN usually does not choose each viewer's quality. It caches the manifest and media segments and serves them from nearby edge locations. The player selects segment URLs and therefore indirectly drives which objects the CDN sees. A manifest may be personalized or signed, while the media segments can be shared cache objects. Keep cache keys stable and include only request dimensions that change the object. A per-viewer token in every segment query can fragment caches; authorization can instead be enforced with signed cookies, path-scoped tokens, or edge validation designed to preserve cache sharing. Ensure the authorization boundary is consistent across manifests, segments, subtitles, and keys.

Cache immutable segments for long periods using versioned paths. Manifests for VOD can also be immutable after publication. Live manifests change frequently and need short freshness or revalidation policies. Origin shielding and request coalescing can reduce a surge against origin when a popular segment is first requested, but they do not replace correct cache headers. If a segment is missing at origin, return a clear failure rather than caching an accidental error as a successful object.

Measure startup delay, rebuffer ratio, average bitrate, quality switches, segment fetch latency, CDN hit ratio, origin bandwidth, and errors by device and geography. Test low bandwidth, sudden bandwidth drop, high RTT, cache cold starts, expired authorization, and missing segments. The central separation is useful: player adaptation optimizes each viewing session; CDN placement and caching reduce delivery cost and latency across sessions.

## Design review

Are segment boundaries aligned across representations? What signals drive the client's bitrate choice? Which objects are immutable? Can the CDN cache media across viewers while still enforcing entitlement? How are live manifests kept fresh without making every segment a miss?

# Signed URLs, DRM, and video security

Video security combines entitlement checks, short-lived delivery authorization, encryption, and operational controls. It helps to separate three goals: stop casual unauthorized access, limit sharing of account credentials or links, and protect high-value media against copying. A signed URL or cookie can address the first two to a degree; DRM may be required for the third. No browser delivery mechanism can guarantee that a viewer cannot capture content that they are authorized to watch.

## Authorize the playback session

The client asks the application to start playback for an asset. The service checks account entitlement, geographic or device policy, concurrent session limits, and any subscription state. It returns a short-lived token scoped to the asset and playback path. Tokens should have an expiry, audience, and signature; validate them at an edge or gateway that protects both the manifest and every segment, subtitle, and encryption key endpoint. A URL containing a bearer token can leak through browser history, analytics, referrer headers, support screenshots, or logs. Prefer short expiry, path restriction, careful redaction, and signed cookies or headers when they fit the client and CDN model.

Authorization and cache identity are related but distinct. If every viewer's token becomes part of the CDN cache key, the same segment may be stored many times and hit ratio can collapse. The edge can validate a token while caching the object by its immutable media path, provided authorization occurs before returning the cached bytes. Test this behavior explicitly: a valid token must not allow a later request without authorization to reuse a cached response. CloudFront cache and origin request policies distinguish cache-key values from values simply sent to origin; similar distinctions exist at other CDNs.

## Add encryption and DRM deliberately

For encrypted media, packaging encrypts segments and publishes key identifiers; an entitled player obtains a license from a license service. W3C Encrypted Media Extensions defines browser APIs for encrypted playback and application-controlled license exchange, but does not itself define a DRM system or guarantee a particular protection level. A license request should bind to the asset, account, device or session policy, and a short validity window as needed. Keep content keys out of application logs and general-purpose data stores; use a dedicated key-management boundary and audited key rotation. Encryption at rest and TLS in transit protect storage and transport, while DRM controls key release to supported playback environments. These are different layers.

Design for platform diversity: browsers and devices may support different key systems, codecs, and robustness modes. Decide whether the product falls back to clear or lower-protection media on unsupported devices; make that policy explicit. Protect license endpoints from replay and abuse with authenticated requests, rate limits, nonce or session binding where supported, and monitoring. Revocation is limited once a client already has a usable key, so short license duration and key rotation windows matter.

Monitor authorization denials, token validation latency, license failures by platform, suspicious session fanout, and playback start failures. Test expired tokens against cached segments, cross-title token reuse, path traversal, clock skew, account cancellation, and license-service outage. Fail closed for protected assets, but provide clear client errors and an operational recovery path. Security quality depends on the full chain—entitlement, edge validation, manifest, segment, and key—not just on signing one playback URL.

## Design review

Is every media object protected by the same entitlement decision? Does edge authorization happen before a cache hit is returned? What leaks bearer tokens through logs or referrers? Which threat requires DRM, and what happens on unsupported devices or license-service failure?

# Live streaming, WebRTC, and latency

“Live” describes a range of latency budgets. A broadcast where viewers can be tens of seconds behind can use segmented HTTP delivery and scale through caches; an interactive call where participants must react within a few hundred milliseconds needs a real-time media path. Picking the protocol follows the product's latency and audience shape, not the label “live.” WebRTC supports interactive media and data exchange; HLS or DASH generally serves large one-to-many audiences more efficiently, often with higher latency.

## Broadcast pipeline versus interactive path

A broadcast pipeline ingests a contribution feed, normalizes or transcodes it, packages short segments and a frequently updated playlist, then distributes those objects through a CDN. The player requests the playlist and segments over HTTP. Shorter segments and more frequent playlist updates can reduce delay, but increase request rate, encoding constraints, and sensitivity to jitter. Low-latency variants use partial segments or chunked transfer patterns and require compatible packagers, CDNs, and players. The end-to-end delay includes capture, encode, ingest, transcode, packaging, origin/CDN propagation, player buffer, and decode. Measure glass-to-glass latency rather than optimizing only segment duration.

For interactive communication, peers first exchange session descriptions and network candidates through an application signaling channel. ICE gathers candidate paths and checks connectivity; STUN helps discover reachable mapped addresses, while TURN relays traffic when direct paths fail. A relay increases bandwidth cost and can add latency, but improves connectivity across restrictive NATs and firewalls. The media path should adapt to packet loss, jitter, and available bandwidth; congestion control and pacing matter as much as codec selection. A selective forwarding unit (SFU) receives participant streams and forwards selected layers to recipients, which usually scales group calls better than every participant sending to every other participant. A mixer decodes and recombines streams but has different compute and layout tradeoffs.

## Match topology to audience

Small interactive groups can use an SFU with simulcast or scalable video coding so each recipient receives an appropriate layer. Large audiences are often better served by a broadcast pipeline and CDN, or by a hybrid where a real-time host feed is repackaged for mass delivery. A WebRTC viewer fanout tree still consumes relay and egress bandwidth and requires session-aware infrastructure; it does not gain the same static segment caching behavior as HTTP delivery. A hybrid can send low-latency WebRTC to hosts and moderators while a larger HLS audience accepts delay.

Capacity planning should include ingest bitrate, transcode profiles, egress per viewer, TURN relay percentage, regions, and failover headroom. Keep signaling separate from media transport: signaling can reconnect or move between servers while an established media path has its own state. Regional placement reduces round-trip time; however, failover can interrupt a call if media state cannot migrate. Track join success, time to first frame, glass-to-glass delay, jitter, packet loss, rebuffering, relay ratio, and bitrate by region and device.

Test UDP blocked, symmetric NAT, relay overload, packet loss, encoder slowdown, stale playlists, and CDN propagation delays. The product should define a latency target and audience size so architecture can choose between cached segments, SFU forwarding, or a deliberate hybrid.

## Design review

What is the latency budget from capture to display? Is the audience interactive or primarily watching? What share of calls require TURN? Does the broadcast pipeline have a player buffer that dominates delay? Which metrics reveal the user-perceived experience?

# Remote file sync design

File synchronization keeps multiple devices convergent while users edit offline, reconnect intermittently, or make concurrent changes. The service should define what “same file” means before choosing its protocol. For ordinary documents, synchronization can exchange whole-file versions or changed blocks; for collaborative structured documents, operation-based CRDT or OT semantics may be needed. A sync engine should make durable versions, conflict behavior, and deletion visible rather than silently overwriting data.

## Model identity, versions, and change feed

Assign each logical file a stable file ID independent of its path. Paths and folder membership can change without changing content identity. Maintain a monotonically increasing server revision or opaque version token, plus metadata such as size, content hash, modification time, and parent folder. Devices remember the last acknowledged cursor or revision. On reconnect, they ask for changes after that cursor; the server returns a bounded ordered change feed with tombstones for deletions and moves. Cursors need retention and expiration rules: if a client is too far behind, require a rescan or snapshot instead of returning an incomplete history.

For each local edit, the client creates an upload intent linked to the base version it edited. The server stores the new content as an immutable blob, then commits metadata using compare-and-set against that base version. If the current version still matches, publish the new revision. If not, preserve both candidates and report a conflict, or apply a domain-specific merge. Never accept “last writer wins” accidentally based on unsynchronized device clocks. A simple conflict copy is often safer than data loss; better merge semantics can be layered for formats where a merge is valid.

## Efficient, resumable transfer

Small files can transfer as whole objects. Large files benefit from chunking and content hashes so unchanged blocks can be reused. Uploads should be resumable and idempotent: each block has a stable content identity, retries do not create duplicate logical changes, and the manifest commits only after all required data exists. Download clients can ask for missing blocks and verify hashes before assembling the file. This reduces bandwidth but introduces metadata, garbage collection, and consistency work; simple whole-file transfer may be preferable when files are small or rarely edited.

Treat the change feed and blob store as separate planes. Metadata transactions decide which version is current; blobs are immutable and may arrive before they are referenced. A background collector removes unreferenced blobs after a safety interval and after accounting for in-flight upload sessions. Keep metadata durable and regionally replicated according to the product's recovery objective. If the feed is unavailable, devices can continue local edits and retry; use bounded exponential backoff and show sync state to users.

Measure sync lag, time to converge, conflict rate, bytes transferred per logical byte changed, cursor resets, failed hash verification, and unreferenced data. Test simultaneous edits, move plus edit, delete while offline, replayed upload, stale cursor, partial chunk arrival, and client clock skew. A sync contract should specify conflict outcomes and retention, since these affect user trust more than transfer speed.

## Design review

What stable identity survives a rename? How does a client resume from a durable cursor? Which concurrent edits merge, and which produce a conflict copy? Are blobs immutable and verified? How does garbage collection avoid deleting in-flight or referenced content?
