# Fixed-block chunking and content addressing

Chunking divides a file into smaller units so clients can upload or download only the pieces that changed. In fixed-block chunking, boundaries occur at regular byte offsets. A manifest records the ordered block identifiers and total file properties. The client hashes each block, asks the server which hashes are already present, and uploads only missing blocks. The new file version is a small manifest that references its blocks. This saves bandwidth when edits preserve block alignment, but inserting bytes near the beginning shifts every later boundary and can make most blocks appear changed.

## Block size and transfer behavior

Small blocks improve deduplication for localized edits and make retries cheaper, but they create many hashes, index entries, requests, and manifest references. Large blocks reduce metadata and request overhead, but one small edit can force retransmission of more bytes. Choose a default based on file size distribution, edit patterns, network RTT, and storage economics; a tiered size policy can prevent tiny files from producing oversized metadata. The client can batch existence checks and missing-block uploads to avoid a round trip per block.

Content addressing names an immutable block by a cryptographic digest of its bytes. Equal blocks can be stored once and referenced from many manifests. Verify the digest on receipt, and use a modern collision-resistant hash for identity. A digest detects accidental corruption; it does not authorize the caller to read or reference a block. Authorization still comes from the account and manifest layer. If blocks are encrypted before hashing, deduplication is scoped to identical ciphertext, and deterministic encryption can leak equality; if the service hashes plaintext, it learns content equality. The privacy and deduplication tradeoff must be explicit.

## Publish manifests safely

Upload missing blocks to an immutable namespace first, then commit the version manifest only after every referenced block is present and verified. The metadata transaction makes the new version visible atomically. Readers should see either the old manifest or the complete new one. Keep manifests bounded and validate block count, lengths, order, and total size. A malicious client could otherwise reference the same block many times to create a huge logical file or force pathological reads. The storage service should reject unreferenced blocks from users without quota and ownership checks, even if the digest is valid.

Garbage collection is harder because blocks may be shared across versions and uploads may be in flight. Mark-and-sweep can trace retained manifests and delete unreferenced blocks only after a grace period that exceeds upload and transaction delays. Reference counts can make deletion faster, but concurrent updates, crashes, and retry duplication can corrupt counts unless operations are transactional or reconciled. Keep a background audit that recomputes reachability for a sample or partition.

Measure bytes saved, unique-block ratio, manifest size, lookup and upload round trips, hash verification failures, and orphan retention. Test an insertion at byte zero, an overwrite within one block, duplicate uploads, stale manifests, hash mismatch, and client crash before commit. Fixed boundaries are simple and predictable; use them when edit alignment is acceptable, and compare them against rolling or content-defined chunking for workloads with frequent insertions.

## Design review

What block size balances request overhead and retry cost? Which layer computes and verifies digests? Does encryption permit or prohibit cross-file deduplication? Are manifests bounded and atomically published? Can garbage collection see in-flight uploads and retained versions?

# Blocklist versioned file metadata

Block-based file storage separates file bytes from the metadata that says how to reconstruct a particular version. A blocklist is the ordered sequence of block identities and lengths for one file revision. The version metadata also carries the file's logical ID, parent or path, size, modification information, and previous revision or lineage. Treat each version's blocklist as immutable: edits create a new version record that reuses unchanged blocks and points to new blocks for changed data.

## Version metadata is the commit record

The upload client first ensures all newly needed blocks exist and are verified. It then submits a new blocklist with the base revision it edited. The metadata service checks authorization, validates that each block is available to the account or permitted namespace, verifies aggregate size and block count, and conditionally commits against the base revision. If another device has already advanced the file, the commit conflicts rather than silently replacing newer metadata. The service can preserve both versions or create a conflict copy according to product policy. A successful commit assigns a server revision and updates the folder's change feed.

This ordering means bytes may exist without being referenced; that is a harmless temporary orphan. The inverse is dangerous: metadata must never point at missing or unverified blocks. The metadata transaction should therefore publish only after storage acknowledgements and validation. If the metadata database update times out, the client queries by an idempotency key or proposed revision ID before retrying; otherwise it may create duplicate versions. Use server time for ordering and a logical revision or sequence rather than trusting client modification timestamps as concurrency control.

## Paths, tombstones, and history

Keep file identity separate from paths so rename and move operations can update directory metadata without rewriting the content blocklist. A folder listing can return a stable revision token and paginated entries. Sync clients consume a change log of creates, updates, moves, and tombstones. Tombstones must remain long enough for offline devices to learn about deletion; purging a tombstone too soon can cause an old client to resurrect the file. Version history policy determines which old blocklists remain roots for garbage collection. Retention and user-visible restore windows should be explicit.

Block references create a reachability graph: current file versions, retained history, shared folders, snapshots, and active upload intents can all keep a block alive. Garbage collection should remove a block only after it is unreachable from every protected root for a grace period. Reference counts can accelerate this but require repair after partial transaction failures; periodic mark-and-sweep provides a correctness check. When deleting a file, first commit a tombstone and remove it from the current namespace, then retire old versions according to retention policy, then allow block reclamation.

Index metadata for files, folders, and revisions by account and parent to serve listings and access checks. Avoid storing one gigantic blocklist in a hot relational row if files can have millions of blocks; use bounded manifests or paged structures with a stable root hash. Measure metadata commit latency, conflict frequency, blocklist size, orphan bytes, GC lag, and stale-client resyncs. Test concurrent upload, move during content update, deletion while offline, metadata timeout after commit, and garbage collection during a pending upload.

## Design review

Can a version commit only after all referenced bytes are durable? What compare-and-set prevents lost updates? How do renames and deletions propagate to offline devices? Which old versions remain GC roots? How does retry after a timed-out metadata commit avoid duplicate revisions?

# Observability for distributed systems

Observability is the ability to explain system behavior from emitted evidence, including situations the team did not predict in advance. In a distributed system, a single user action crosses processes, queues, databases, and networks. No one host log can tell the whole story. A useful design combines metrics for aggregate shape, traces for request paths, and logs or events for detailed facts, with shared resource and request context that lets an operator move between them.

## Instrument the user journey

Start from important user-visible operations and define what success, latency, and failure mean for each. Record request counts and outcomes, latency distributions, saturation, and queue depth at service boundaries. Histograms are usually more useful than averages because they preserve tail behavior; alerting on p95 or p99 latency can show pain hidden by a healthy mean. Metrics need bounded dimensions. Service, operation, region, and status class are often useful; raw user IDs, request IDs, or arbitrary URLs can create unbounded time series and high cost. Put unique identifiers in trace or log fields instead.

Trace context should propagate across RPC and asynchronous boundaries. A trace can show that the API returned quickly while the queue waited ten minutes, or that one database dependency dominated a request. For queues, record producer and consumer spans with message correlation, and preserve the causal link even when the work runs later. Sampling keeps telemetry volume manageable, but head sampling may drop the exact rare slow request that matters. Tail sampling can retain traces based on duration or error, at additional collector state and cost. Keep a controlled path for high-severity traces and record sampling decisions.

Logs capture discrete events and context that do not fit a metric. Use stable structured fields and include trace and span identifiers where available. Do not log secrets, credentials, full payment data, or unnecessary personal information. A syntactically JSON record is not automatically a stable schema; field names and types need conventions. Include enough context to diagnose an event without turning logs into an unbounded copy of every request body.

## Make telemetry reliable and affordable

Telemetry export must not become a synchronous dependency on the user request. Buffer locally with bounded queues, batch exports, and define what happens when the collector or backend is unavailable. Under pressure, drop low-value debug data before blocking application work. Monitor the observability pipeline itself: dropped spans, collector queue utilization, scrape failures, ingest delay, cardinality, and cost. A dashboard that is stale or silently missing one region is an operational hazard.

Dashboards should answer a small set of questions quickly: is the service serving users, where is latency coming from, and is the system approaching capacity? Alert on symptoms and actionable conditions, not every internal metric crossing an arbitrary threshold. The four golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, and saturation—are a useful starting point, but asynchronous systems also need queue age and consumer lag; storage systems need replication and disk health; control planes need convergence and reconciliation status.

Exercise the path by injecting an error or a slow dependency and confirming that the event appears in a dashboard, alert, trace, and log with consistent context. Track time to detect and diagnose, not just telemetry volume. Observability is a product capability: teams should be able to ask a new diagnostic question without deploying emergency instrumentation during an incident.

## Design review

Can an operator follow a request across services and queues? Which metric dimensions are bounded? How are traces sampled without hiding rare failures? What happens when telemetry export is down? Are sensitive values excluded, and is the telemetry pipeline monitored like production infrastructure?

# SLOs and error budgets

A service level objective (SLO) is a measurable target for a user-relevant aspect of service quality over a stated window. It turns vague goals like “fast and reliable” into a decision tool for engineering and product teams. An SLO is built from a service level indicator (SLI), such as the fraction of eligible requests that succeed or finish under a latency threshold, and a target such as 99.9% over 28 days. The error budget is the allowed unreliability: one minus the objective.

## Choose indicators users can feel

Define the request population and exclusions precisely. If health checks or internal retries count differently, document the reason. A successful HTTP status may still represent failure if the response is unusable; a cache hit could still be stale; a background job may be “available” while delayed beyond its deadline. For latency, decide whether the SLI is a threshold fraction, a percentile, or a user-journey duration. For batch work, completion within an agreed age may be more meaningful than per-request latency. Measure at the boundary that approximates what the user observes and validate it against client-side evidence.

Use event-based SLIs when requests are independently countable, or time-based SLIs when the service is judged by intervals of healthy operation. Event-based ratios avoid a quiet period looking healthy just because there were few measurements. Split objectives only when different user journeys genuinely have different expectations. Too many SLOs create policy noise; too few hide which audience is harmed. A service may have an availability SLO and a latency SLO, but each needs an accountable owner, data source, and alert path.

## Spend budget intentionally

If a 99.9% objective is measured over a month, the remaining 0.1% is the budget for bad events in that window. The budget is not a target to consume; it is a way to balance release speed and reliability investment. A team can set policy that normal changes proceed while budget remains, but repeated or fast budget burn pauses risky changes and directs capacity toward mitigation. The response should be based on user impact and cause, not punishment. A dependency outage can spend the service's budget even when application code is healthy, which gives a reason to reduce dependency risk or adjust the dependency contract.

Use both a long rolling window and a short burn-rate alert. A slow degradation may consume budget over weeks; a sharp outage may exhaust it in hours. Multi-window burn alerts catch urgent incidents while reducing noise from brief blips. Budget accounting should be transparent and robust to telemetry gaps. If the SLI pipeline fails, mark budget data as unknown rather than treating missing events as successful requests. Avoid changing an objective retroactively to erase a miss; revise it forward with documented reasoning and stakeholder agreement.

Review objectives against actual user expectations and product economics. A database-backed internal tool may not need the same availability as checkout. Conversely, a high SLO that costs heavily to achieve without changing user outcomes may be wasteful. Use error budget reports to prioritize investments such as graceful degradation, dependency isolation, rollout controls, and repair automation. Track objective attainment, budget burn, and outcome of reliability work, not just uptime claims.

## Design review

Is the SLI user-centered and precisely defined? Does the denominator represent real eligible traffic? Are short and long burn windows actionable? What policy follows when the budget is nearly spent? How are telemetry gaps and external dependency failures represented?

# Incident response

Incident response is a coordinated way to reduce user harm while preserving enough information to understand what happened. It is a system design problem because safe recovery depends on clear ownership, observable state, reversible controls, and dependencies that can be isolated. During an incident, the first job is to restore a safe level of service; detailed root-cause analysis can follow once the system is stable.

## Establish a simple command structure

When impact is broad or uncertain, name an incident lead who coordinates the response, an operations lead who runs technical mitigation, and a communications lead who updates stakeholders. One person can fill multiple roles in a small event, but make the responsibilities explicit. Keep a shared timeline with timestamps, observations, hypotheses, actions, and outcomes. This reduces duplicate work and makes shift handoff possible. Assign tasks by owner and expected update time; avoid several people independently changing the same production control.

Triage from user symptoms and service objectives: which journeys fail, how many users, which regions, and what changed? Compare recent deployments, configuration, dependency health, queue lag, saturation, and error rates. Use traces and logs to localize the path, but verify that the signal is current and covers the affected population. Establish an initial severity based on impact, not on how easy the technical cause seems. If evidence is incomplete, mitigate conservatively and state uncertainty.

## Prefer reversible mitigation

Choose controls that reduce impact quickly and can be rolled back: disable a feature flag, shed optional work, shift traffic, pause a rollout, scale a constrained pool, or fail over to a known-good dependency. Understand secondary effects before acting: routing all traffic away from a region can overload the remaining regions, and retry storms can amplify an outage. Use idempotent, auditable operations where possible. Make one change at a time when practical, then check the expected user-facing signal before continuing. A rollback may not reverse a database migration or external side effect, so identify those risks before triggering it.

Protect responders from fatigue and information overload. Keep one incident channel as the source of truth, publish concise updates at a predictable cadence, and rotate people for long events. Do not page every team for every alert; route alerts to the owner who can act. If a mitigation is uncertain, stop risky changes and preserve evidence. Once service is restored, verify recovery across regions, clients, queues, and dependent workflows; a green dashboard can hide a growing backlog.

## Learn and close the loop

Afterward, write a blameless review focused on contributing conditions and missing defenses. Include the user impact timeline, detection and mitigation gaps, what went well, and a small set of owned actions with dates. Actions should reduce recurrence or impact—for example, add a canary, cap retries, improve a dashboard, or make a failover safe. Track completion and verify the change; a postmortem without follow-through is an archive, not a reliability mechanism. Share relevant details with support and affected users according to the communication policy.

Practice response with game days and realistic failure drills. Include alert receipt, access to runbooks, dependency ownership, rollback, and communications. Measure time to detect, acknowledge, mitigate, and recover, but use these metrics to improve the system rather than grade individuals. The response process should remain usable when chat, dashboards, or the primary region are themselves impaired.

## Design review

Who coordinates decisions and communications? Which mitigations are reversible? Can one action overload a surviving region or amplify retries? How is recovery verified beyond the first green graph? Are follow-up actions owned and tested?

# Deployment and migration safety

Deployment safety is the ability to change software while limiting the size and duration of mistakes. A release should be observable, staged, and reversible at the level of traffic and behavior. “Rollback” is not always a binary operation: code can be rolled back quickly, while a schema change or emitted event may already have made data incompatible with the previous version. Plan compatibility before deployment rather than treating rollback as an afterthought.

## Reduce blast radius

Build an immutable artifact once and promote the same artifact through test, canary, and production stages. Validate configuration separately and record the exact artifact and configuration revision used by each environment. A canary receives a small representative share of traffic or a limited worker cohort. Compare error rate, latency, saturation, and business outcomes to a control group, accounting for traffic mix and time effects. Halt promotion automatically when a guardrail fails. A canary that only checks process liveness can miss incorrect responses or data corruption.

Feature flags separate deployment from activation. They can release a dark code path to production, then enable it for internal users or a percentage of traffic. Flags need owners, expiry, and a cleanup process; forgotten flags become permanent branching complexity. A flag does not protect against database writes already issued by the new code, so data compatibility remains necessary. Progressive delivery can use percentage rollout, region by region, or one service instance at a time depending on statefulness and traffic distribution.

## Make old and new versions coexist

For an API or event schema change, use an expand-and-contract sequence: first add the new field or table in a backward-compatible way; deploy readers that understand both forms; begin writing the new form; backfill existing data; validate parity; switch reads; and only later remove the old form after old clients and workers are gone. This sequence handles mixed versions during rolling deployment. A destructive rename or type change in one step can break an old binary that remains active during the rollout.

Backfills should be resumable, rate-limited, checkpointed, and observable. They compete with user traffic for database resources and can create replication lag. Run them in bounded batches, monitor lock time and query load, and make each batch idempotent. Before the cutover, define a consistency check and a stop condition. If the new path is incorrect, an explicit rollback or forward-fix plan should account for writes made during the transition.

## Verify through the full release

Pre-production tests reduce risk but cannot prove production health. Use a canary, automated health gates, and an operator-visible rollout status. Keep a kill switch for dangerous optional behavior, but verify that disabling it does not strand in-flight work. Avoid coupling multiple unrelated risky changes in one release; if metrics regress, smaller changes make attribution easier. Store release events alongside telemetry so operators can correlate regressions with exact changes.

Track deployment frequency, change failure rate, time to restore, canary aborts, migration lag, and rollback success. Test a release where one region lags, a worker runs an old schema reader, and a backfill is interrupted. The safest deployment is not necessarily the slowest: clear compatibility, small blast radius, and automatic evidence allow changes to proceed with controlled risk.

## Design review

Can old and new binaries coexist against the schema and events? Is the canary representative and tied to user outcomes? Can a backfill pause and resume safely? What irreversible writes occur before rollback? Which gate stops promotion and who can override it?

- [Martin Fowler: parallel change](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html)
- [Martin Fowler: feature toggles](https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html)

# Database migration safety

Database schema changes are production releases because application versions overlap, tables may be large, and a DDL statement can hold locks or rewrite data. Safe migration design starts by asking which old and new binaries will run at the same time, what locks the database takes, and how long a backfill competes with live traffic. A migration that succeeds quickly on a small staging table can block production writers for minutes or hours.

## Expand, migrate, contract

For a rename or type change, avoid a one-step destructive edit. Add a new nullable field or compatible structure first. Deploy code that can read the old and new forms, and initially continue writing the old form if necessary. Then dual-write or switch writes in a controlled phase, backfill existing rows in batches, compare values, and move reads to the new representation. Only after all binaries, jobs, and clients stop using the old field should a later release remove it. This lets rolling deploys, delayed workers, and rollback coexist with the schema transition.

Backfills should be restartable and idempotent. Process bounded primary-key ranges, persist a checkpoint, throttle based on replica lag and database load, and expose rows completed and remaining. Avoid one huge transaction that holds locks, bloats the write-ahead log, or makes rollback expensive. Define how concurrent updates are handled: the backfill must not overwrite a value written by new code. A condition on the old value or change-data capture can close the race, followed by a reconciliation query.

## Understand lock and rewrite behavior

Read the database engine's documentation for the exact version in production. A statement that appears metadata-only may still need a strong lock briefly; adding a constraint can scan the whole table; changing a type can rewrite it; and creating an index can block writes unless an online option is used. In PostgreSQL, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` reduces write blocking but performs additional work, can fail and leave an invalid index, and cannot run inside a transaction block. Some migration frameworks wrap every migration in a transaction, so the framework and DDL behavior must be considered together. Use short lock and statement timeouts so a migration fails rather than queueing behind a busy transaction and blocking subsequent traffic.

Split schema declaration, data movement, and cleanup into separate operations with observable checkpoints. For constraints, some databases allow adding the constraint without immediate validation and validating separately, reducing impact on concurrent updates. Monitor locks, waiters, query latency, replication lag, disk use, and progress while the migration runs. Ensure free disk can accommodate temporary indexes or table copies.

Before running a migration, rehearse it on production-shaped data and record expected duration and lock behavior. Have a stop rule and a forward recovery plan. Rolling back application code may be simple; reversing transformed or deleted data may not be. Keep backups and verify restore procedures, but do not confuse a backup with a fast migration rollback. The safest schema change is one that can pause at every phase while old and new code continue to function.

## Design review

Which application versions are compatible at each phase? Does the DDL scan, rewrite, or lock the table? Can the backfill pause, resume, and avoid overwriting concurrent writes? How is completion validated before removing the old schema? What is the recovery plan if cleanup has already started?

# Parallel monolith read drain

Moving a capability out of a monolith is safer when the old and new paths can run side by side and traffic can move gradually. A read drain is a useful first step: keep the monolith as the source of truth for writes, mirror or replicate the relevant data to the new service, compare responses, then route selected reads to the new service. This limits the risk because a read can usually be retried or sent back to the old implementation without creating duplicate side effects.

## Establish data parity before switching

Put a routing facade in front of the capability so callers use one stable API while the implementation changes behind it. Define ownership for each record and which database is authoritative at every stage. Use an initial snapshot followed by change-data capture or another ordered change feed to keep the new store current. Track source offsets and replication lag. A “dual read” can compare old and new results on sampled requests, but do not return both or let one path mutate state. Compare normalized semantics, not only JSON shape: ordering, null handling, access control, and freshness may differ.

Begin by shadowing a small percentage of reads to the new service while still returning the monolith response. Shadow traffic must be bounded so it does not double load a fragile database, and it must avoid side effects such as billing, notifications, or audit writes. Redact sensitive data and apply normal authorization to the shadow request. Record mismatches by category and enough identifiers to diagnose without logging full private payloads. Do not promote while differences remain unexplained.

## Shift traffic and drain dependencies

When parity and latency are acceptable, route a small percentage of real reads to the new service, keeping a fast fallback to the monolith. Increase traffic gradually by tenant, region, or percentage. Watch error rate, tail latency, stale-read complaints, database load, and fallback rate. Fallback must have a deadline and circuit breaker; otherwise a degraded new service can send all traffic back to the monolith and overload it. Keep the old path alive until the rollback window and data consistency checks are complete.

The cutover is not finished merely because requests route elsewhere. Find batch jobs, admin tools, caches, reporting queries, and background workers that still read the monolith tables. Add ownership metadata and access logging to identify clients. Drain these dependencies deliberately and remove old credentials only after they no longer have legitimate use. If the new service becomes the write owner, plan a separate write migration with idempotency, dual-write consistency, conflict resolution, and rollback semantics. Reads are often reversible; writes across two databases are not automatically safe.

Keep a tested kill switch and preserve the old binary and schema until traffic is fully drained. Record every stage and its stop condition. A migration is successful when the old service can be removed without hidden consumers, stale data, or an unplanned fallback dependency. Metrics should include shadow coverage, mismatch rate, replication lag, traffic percentage, fallback rate, and remaining monolith callers.

## Design review

Which store is authoritative during each phase? Does the shadow path avoid side effects and extra load? How is semantic parity measured? Can fallback overload the old service? What inventory proves that all reads have drained before the old path is removed?

# Backups and restore

A backup is useful only if it can be restored within the time and data-loss limits the business accepts. Backup design should begin with recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum tolerable loss of recent writes, and recovery time objective (RTO), the maximum acceptable restoration duration. Those targets determine backup frequency, log retention, replication, storage location, and the amount of automation required. “We have snapshots” is not a recovery objective.

## Select a recovery method

Logical exports are portable and can restore selected tables or records, but may be slow for large datasets. Physical snapshots restore database files quickly but can be engine- and version-specific. Continuous log archiving or point-in-time recovery can reduce data loss between snapshots, provided logs are retained and replay order is valid. Replicas can promote quickly for some failures but may copy accidental deletion or corruption immediately, so they are not a substitute for independent backups. A tiered plan can combine frequent transaction logs with periodic full backups and isolated copies.

Backups need consistency across related state. If the service stores database metadata and object blobs separately, a database snapshot and blob inventory taken at different times may not describe the same logical moment. Use immutable object versions, snapshot coordination, or a recovery manifest that identifies the corresponding data boundary. Include configuration, encryption keys, access policies, and deployment artifacts required to make restored data usable. Protect keys independently but ensure the recovery team can access them during a regional failure.

## Protect and verify copies

Keep at least one copy outside the primary failure domain and restrict deletion permissions. Immutability or object lock can protect against compromised credentials and ransomware. Encrypt backups and audit access, but do not let key loss make the backup unrecoverable. Verify checksums after transfer and store backup catalogs in a separate, durable location. Retention policy should reflect legal and product requirements; backups can retain deleted personal data beyond the primary system's deletion window, so deletion and restore procedures must account for that.

Restore tests should be scheduled, not improvised during an outage. Restore into an isolated environment, validate database integrity and application-level invariants, replay logs to a chosen point, and measure actual time. A successful cloud snapshot operation only proves that a snapshot was created. It does not prove that the backup can be decrypted, mounted, replayed, or used by the current application. Test partial recovery for accidental row deletion as well as full-region recovery.

Track last successful backup age, log archive lag, backup size and growth, checksum failures, restore duration, and test coverage. Alert when the newest recoverable point exceeds the RPO or when a retention gap appears. Document who can declare recovery, where credentials live, and how clients reconnect after restore. Recovery targets should be tested against the whole service, including DNS, secrets, queues, and external integrations.

## Design review

What RPO and RTO are promised? Are backups consistent across database and blob state? Is a copy protected from the same account compromise as production? Can current operators restore and validate a point in time? How do deletion obligations interact with retained backups?

# Disaster recovery

Disaster recovery (DR) restores service after a failure that removes a substantial part of the normal production environment, such as a region outage, account compromise, or data-center loss. It differs from high availability: HA handles smaller failures automatically within the normal operating environment, while DR may require a deliberate activation, data recovery, and traffic cutover. Define recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) for each critical user journey, then choose a strategy that meets those objectives at an acceptable cost.

## Choose a recovery topology

Backup and restore keeps a separate copy of data and recreates infrastructure after failure. It is cost-efficient but often has the longest RTO. Pilot light keeps core data replication and minimal infrastructure warm, then scales services after activation. Warm standby runs a reduced but functional copy and can cut over faster at higher cost. Active-active serves traffic from multiple regions, but adds consistency, routing, and operational complexity. These are points on a cost and recovery spectrum, not labels that guarantee a specific RTO.

Replicate the state needed to serve requests, not just the main database. This may include object storage, encryption keys, identity configuration, secrets, container images, DNS records, queues, feature flags, and required external service credentials. Infrastructure as code reduces manual recreation errors, but the recovery environment must be tested with the exact production configuration and quotas. Cross-region replication can lag or replicate corruption; define which data is authoritative and how operators choose the last safe recovery point.

## Failover without a split brain

Before shifting traffic, determine whether the original region is truly unavailable or merely isolated from the control plane. If both regions can accept writes, clients may create conflicting histories. Use a clear writer-election or fencing mechanism: the old region must be prevented from writing before the recovery region becomes authoritative. DNS TTLs and client caches can delay traffic movement; health checks need to distinguish user-serving health from an endpoint that only answers TCP. After failover, preserve the old environment for forensic analysis and avoid automatic failback until data has been reconciled.

Recovery playbooks should define authority, technical steps, decision thresholds, communications, and validation queries. Run game days that exercise full cutover, including application secrets, queues, search indexes, object access, and third-party dependencies. Measure actual recovery time and data loss against the targets. Test both a planned regional evacuation and a scenario where the primary is unreachable and its final writes are unknown. A recovery that restores compute but not authorization or user-visible data is incomplete.

After the primary returns, reconciling divergent data and switching back can be riskier than failover. Treat failback as a separate planned migration: establish a new source of truth, replicate in one direction, validate parity, and move traffic gradually. Keep the DR topology simple enough that an on-call team can operate it under stress. Review objectives after major architecture or business changes, and retain evidence from exercises.

## Design review

What failure domain does the plan cover? Which state is replicated and with what lag? How is the old writer fenced before promotion? Has end-to-end RTO been measured in a real exercise? What exact reconciliation process governs failback?

# Data retention, deletion, and privacy

Retention and deletion are core data lifecycle operations. Keeping every event forever increases breach impact, storage cost, and legal exposure; deleting immediately can break billing, audit, safety, or user recovery requirements. Start by classifying data by purpose and sensitivity, assign an owner and retention window, and define what “delete” means across primary storage, indexes, caches, analytics, replicas, and backups. The architecture should make those obligations executable and observable.

## Minimize and map data

Collect only fields required for a named product or operational purpose. Avoid copying personal data into logs, traces, search indexes, exports, and support tools by default. Maintain a data inventory that maps each field to its source of truth, processors, retention period, and deletion mechanism. Data lineage is essential: a user record can fan out into denormalized tables, event streams, object blobs, derived embeddings, and backups. Without that map, a delete request can remove the obvious account row while leaving active copies elsewhere.

Define the difference between deleting an account, removing access, anonymizing a record, and expiring a temporary copy. Some systems need a durable tombstone so delayed consumers do not recreate deleted data. A tombstone should contain the minimum information needed to enforce deletion and should itself have a defined retention period. For event-sourced data, deleting the projection may not remove the source event; the system may need encryption-key destruction, redaction events, or a documented exception based on the data's purpose and obligations. These decisions are domain and jurisdiction specific, so have the accountable privacy and legal owners define the policy.

## Make deletion propagate

Represent a deletion request as a durable workflow with an idempotency key and per-system status. The workflow authenticates the request, checks identity and policy, marks the account as deleting to block new writes, emits an outbox event, and schedules downstream cleanup. Consumers should be idempotent and retryable. Track completion acknowledgements for databases, object stores, search indexes, caches, analytics, and third-party processors. A periodic reconciliation job catches missed or failed consumers. Do not report completion until the defined scope has been processed; if some copies have different expiration behavior, state that clearly in the product policy.

Backups pose a special problem because restoring them can resurrect deleted records. Common designs retain tombstones and replay deletion events after restoration, or apply a deletion ledger before restored data is exposed. Immutable backups may be retained until their scheduled expiry while access is tightly restricted; a restored environment must still process the deletion ledger. Document this behavior and test it. For derived data, deleting the source may require rebuilding a model or index rather than surgically locating every contribution.

Monitor request age, failures by downstream store, tombstone backlog, late writes after deletion, and deletion reconciliation gaps. Test duplicate requests, identity ambiguity, consumer outage, restore from an old backup, and account reactivation during cleanup. Data lifecycle decisions should be reviewed whenever a new system begins storing personal data. Retention is not just a TTL setting: it is a distributed workflow with privacy, correctness, and recovery consequences.

## Design review

Can every copy and derived dataset be discovered? Does deletion block new writes before fanout begins? How are tombstones retained and eventually removed? What happens to a deleted record after backup restore? Can the system prove completion for the defined data scope?

# Security and abuse prevention

Security and abuse prevention work best when they are part of the system's normal request path, not a collection of emergency controls added after launch. Design for authenticated identity, least privilege, explicit authorization, bounded resource use, auditability, and safe failure. Abuse includes more than malicious account takeover: a buggy client, compromised integration, or unexpectedly popular feature can exhaust compute, storage, or paid downstream APIs.

## Enforce identity and authorization at boundaries

Authenticate users and service identities at the edge, then authorize each operation against the resource and tenant. Do not treat an opaque ID or unguessable URL as proof of access. Check ownership at the service boundary and avoid trusting a client-supplied user or tenant field when verified identity context is available. For internal calls, use explicit service identity and scoped permissions rather than one broad shared credential. Rotate secrets, keep them out of source control and telemetry, and record access to sensitive operations.

Use defense in depth: network boundaries, input validation, least-privilege storage policy, encryption, and application checks. A CDN or cache can accidentally bypass authorization if a personalized response is cached under a shared key. Verify access control for cache hits as well as origin misses. For uploads, limit size, type, parsing cost, and access to staging objects. For outbound integrations, constrain destinations and budgets to reduce SSRF and financial abuse. Validate structured inputs with maximum lengths, collection sizes, and allowed formats.

## Bound resource consumption

Every expensive operation should have an explicit budget: request rate, concurrency, payload size, query complexity, retry count, storage, CPU, and downstream spend. Rate limits should account for identity confidence. IP is useful before login and for broad attack suppression, but NAT can group legitimate users. Account or API key limits are more precise after authentication; tenant-level budgets protect shared capacity; endpoint-specific controls protect expensive actions. Layer limits instead of relying on one identifier. Return a consistent throttling response and retry guidance, and avoid revealing sensitive account existence through different error behavior.

Retries and fanout can amplify overload. Use deadlines, bounded exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and queue admission controls. A limit at the gateway can protect the public edge but does not necessarily protect an expensive internal method called by other services. Enforce a final resource budget at the service that owns the cost, with upstream controls for early rejection. Preserve emergency administrative access under strong authentication, separate from user paths, and audit changes to limits.

## Detect and respond

Log security events with stable actor, action, resource, decision, and request context while minimizing sensitive payloads. Detect unusual account, tenant, IP, or key behavior using baselines and high-confidence rules; alerting on every spike will train responders to ignore alerts. Provide controls to revoke sessions, keys, and tokens; quarantine abuse; disable a feature; and preserve evidence. Run tabletop exercises for credential compromise, data exfiltration, abusive automation, and an unexpectedly expensive endpoint.

Measure denied authorization, suspicious rate patterns, resource exhaustion, quota use, secret age, audit coverage, and time to revoke credentials. Test cross-tenant access, replayed capabilities, missing authorization on cache hits, oversized request bodies, and abusive retry loops. Security controls should degrade intentionally: decide whether an unavailable policy store means reject, queue, or allow a request, based on the sensitivity of the operation.

## Design review

Where is identity established and checked? Are limits enforced where expensive resources are consumed? Can a cache return data before authorization? What happens when policy or audit services are unavailable? Can operators rapidly revoke credentials and cap spend?

# Rate limiter placement and keys

A rate limiter decides whether to admit work based on recent usage. The hard architectural questions are where that decision is enforced, which identity the quota follows, and what happens when the limiter state is unavailable. A gateway is a good place to reject obvious excess traffic early, but it may not know the true resource cost or authenticated tenant for every operation. The service that owns an expensive resource should enforce a final limit as well.

## Choose keys that match the policy

An IP-based key can limit anonymous traffic and blunt broad floods, but many legitimate users may share a corporate or mobile carrier address. Account IDs or API keys provide a more product-aligned quota after authentication, but attackers can create accounts or rotate keys. Tenant IDs protect each customer's allocation, while global service budgets protect total capacity. Endpoint or operation keys let expensive actions have stricter limits than cheap reads. A composite decision often checks several dimensions: edge IP burst, authenticated user quota, tenant concurrency, and global dependency budget.

Do not accept the rate-limit identity from an untrusted header. The gateway should remove externally supplied identity headers and insert verified context. Normalize keys consistently across services. Hash or otherwise protect identifiers in limiter telemetry if key disclosure creates privacy risk. Keep the key space bounded; raw URL paths, random tokens, or arbitrary query parameters can create unbounded limiter state. Group endpoints into stable operation classes.

## Place checks along the cost path

At the edge, reject excessive requests before authentication work and application routing. After authentication, enforce account, plan, and tenant quotas. At the service or worker pool, enforce concurrency, queue admission, and expensive-operation budgets. A per-process limiter is fast but each instance has an independent view, so traffic can multiply its effective limit across replicas. A centralized store provides a shared counter but adds network latency and can become a dependency. Local token buckets can absorb bursts while a global limiter enforces a longer-term quota; this hybrid must specify how much overshoot is acceptable.

Rate limits are not the same as concurrency limits. A request rate can stay within quota while slow requests accumulate and exhaust workers. Bound in-flight work with semaphores or queue limits and set deadlines. A queue can smooth bursts but does not remove overload; cap its depth and age, and reject or defer work with an explicit user contract. Return `429` or a domain-specific quota response with retry guidance when the client can safely try again. For service protection, shedding optional work may be preferable to delaying every request.

## Failure and policy behavior

If the shared limiter is unavailable, choose fail-open or fail-closed by operation. A low-risk cached read may allow a small local fallback budget; a costly payment or authentication attempt may fail closed. Alert on limiter errors and fallback activation. Make counter updates atomic so concurrent requests cannot all observe capacity and overshoot unpredictably. Policies should be versioned and distributed consistently; a quota change can cause a sudden client-visible shift.

Track allowed and denied counts by operation and plan, limiter latency, store errors, overshoot, cardinality, and local fallback. Test NAT users, account rotation, autoscaling, clock skew, a limiter outage, hot tenant keys, and a sudden policy reduction. A limit is only useful if the enforcement layer can identify the caller reliably and protect the actual resource at risk.

## Design review

Which limit belongs at the edge, authenticated service, and worker pool? Can a caller spoof the key? Does each instance multiply the allowed rate? What is the fail-open budget? How are concurrency and backlog constrained separately from requests per second?

# Sliding window rate limiter

A sliding window limiter enforces a maximum number of requests over a rolling interval, such as at most 100 operations during any 60 seconds. It avoids the boundary burst of a fixed window, where a client can spend the full quota just before a window resets and again immediately after. Exact rolling windows give a precise decision but require more state and work; approximations trade precision for lower memory and latency.

## Exact log and approximate counter

An exact implementation stores a timestamp for each admitted request per key. On a request, remove timestamps older than the window, count the remaining events, and admit only if the count is below the limit. The decision and insertion must be atomic, or simultaneous requests can all observe the same count and exceed the cap. This is straightforward conceptually but stores O(requests) events and makes cleanup important. It is appropriate for lower-volume or security-sensitive quotas where exactness matters.

A sliding-window counter uses two fixed buckets: the current window and the previous one. It estimates recent usage as current count plus a weighted portion of the previous count based on how far the current interval has progressed. This needs only a small number of counters and can be atomic in a shared store. The estimate is not exact because it assumes requests in the previous bucket were spread uniformly. For a high-volume API quota, that error may be acceptable; for strict financial or safety limits, choose a stronger consistency model or use a token bucket with carefully defined semantics.

Token buckets solve a related but different problem: they allow a configured burst and replenish at a steady rate. A sliding window constrains the total during each rolling period. Product language should say whether a short burst is allowed, since “100 requests per minute” does not fully define behavior. Some systems combine an instantaneous concurrency limit, a burst bucket, and a longer rolling usage budget.

## Distributed atomicity and time

For multiple API instances, state must be shared or overshoot must be bounded. A Redis sorted set can hold exact event times with an atomic script that prunes, counts, and inserts. A two-counter approximation can use atomic increments and expirations. Partition limiter keys to distribute load, but a very hot tenant key can still become a bottleneck. Regional replicas introduce consistency delay: if two regions accept against independent counters, the quota may be exceeded by the sum. Decide whether a limit is global, per-region, or intentionally approximate. Use a single authority or coordinated allocation of quota when hard global enforcement matters.

Use server-side time from a consistent clock source, and store timestamps at adequate precision. Cleanup keys or events after their useful window to bound memory. When a key has no traffic, it should expire naturally. Avoid deleting a current counter early during a policy update, which can reset quota unexpectedly. Version keys or policies deliberately and specify whether the new policy takes effect immediately or at the next window boundary.

Return remaining quota and reset information only if those values are meaningful under the algorithm. A retry-after estimate is useful but not a promise that the exact next request will succeed under concurrent traffic. Test requests clustered at bucket boundaries, parallel admission races, clock movement, store failover, and hot keys. Measure denied requests, overshoot, decision latency, key count, and store load.

## Design review

Is an exact rolling decision required, or is weighted approximation adequate? Are prune/count/insert atomic? What burst semantics does the API promise? How does quota behave across regions? Are state expiry and policy changes safe for active windows?

# Multi-tenant design

Multi-tenant design lets one service operate for many customer organizations while preserving isolation, fair resource use, and a consistent product lifecycle. A tenant is a security and business boundary: requests, stored records, background jobs, caches, and exports must remain scoped to the right organization. The architecture also decides how much infrastructure is shared. Pooling improves utilization; siloing offers stronger resource and data separation; a bridge model combines them for selected layers or customer tiers.

## Carry tenant context end to end

Resolve the tenant from a verified identity or trusted routing domain after authentication. Do not accept an arbitrary tenant ID from the request body as the authorization source. Carry tenant context through service calls, queue messages, scheduled jobs, and audit events. Each consumer should verify that the context is present and authorized for the target object. Database queries should require tenant scope by default, and tests should attempt cross-tenant reads and writes. In pooled tables, tenant ID commonly belongs in the partition or leading index key; database row-level security can add defense in depth but does not replace safe application authorization.

Caches and object storage need equal care. Include tenant identity in cache keys whenever returned data varies by tenant, or separate cache namespaces by tenant. Ensure a CDN does not cache private responses under a shared key. Use opaque storage prefixes and policies that limit access, but do not treat the prefix as the only check. Search indexes, analytics exports, and data warehouses need tenant filters and access controls as well. A single missed path can create a cross-tenant data leak.

## Choose isolation and fairness

In a silo model, each tenant has dedicated resources or storage. This improves isolation and can simplify customer-specific recovery, but increases provisioning, upgrades, and operational cost. In a pool model, tenants share compute and data structures; onboarding and release operations are efficient, but a noisy tenant can affect others and isolation mistakes have a larger blast radius. A bridge model mixes choices—for example shared web services with dedicated databases for high-sensitivity tenants. Choose per component based on data sensitivity, noisy-neighbor risk, scale, compliance needs, and operational capacity rather than making a single all-or-nothing decision.

Enforce fairness with per-tenant rate and concurrency limits, queue partitions, storage quotas, and workload scheduling. A tenant should not monopolize a shared worker pool or hot database partition. Measure usage and capacity by tenant while restricting access to sensitive identifiers. Large-tenant migration between tiers or shards should be a planned operation with routing version, backfill, dual-read validation, and cutover controls.

## Operations and lifecycle

Provisioning, configuration, backups, deletion, and upgrades should be automated through a unified control plane. A dedicated tenant stack still benefits from one product version and one operational experience; otherwise version drift becomes a separate support burden. Track per-tenant errors, latency, usage, quota, and noisy-neighbor impact while maintaining aggregate service objectives. Tenant-aware logs must avoid exposing one tenant's data to another tenant's administrators or support users.

Test tenant context loss across asynchronous boundaries, cache key collisions, query omissions, tenant deletion, a large noisy tenant, and movement from pooled to isolated resources. Include tenant identity in synthetic tests. Review permission models and database policies before adding new storage systems. Multi-tenancy is not achieved by adding a `tenant_id` column alone; it requires consistent isolation and fair scheduling across every layer.

## Design review

Where is tenant identity established and propagated? Which layers pool or silo, and why? How do caches, jobs, search, and exports enforce tenant scope? What limits prevent a noisy tenant from harming others? Can the control plane provision, recover, and delete tenants consistently?

# Design: a URL shortener, one machine

Start with the smallest system that satisfies the behavior: accept a long URL, return a short code, and redirect code lookups to the original destination. One application process and one relational database can handle an early product. The goal is to make correctness explicit before adding scale: codes must be unique, redirects must be fast, invalid URLs must be rejected, and creation retries must not create duplicate links.

## Requirements and data model

For creation, accept a URL, validate scheme and length, apply abuse checks, allocate a code, and persist the mapping. For redirect, look up code, check expiration or disabled status, record any required analytics, and issue an HTTP redirect. A relational table can hold `code` as a primary key, `target_url`, creation time, optional expiration, owner, and status. A unique constraint on code is the final collision guard. Keep analytics separate from the critical redirect transaction if the product does not need synchronous counts; writing one analytics row per redirect can turn the hot path into a write bottleneck.

To generate codes on one machine, use a database sequence and encode the integer in a base-62 alphabet. This produces compact, unique codes within the database's sequence scope. It is predictable, so it may not suit privacy or unguessability requirements; random codes can be used instead, with collision retries protected by the unique constraint. Do not assume a random collision is impossible; catch it and generate another code. The sequence strategy also has a clear capacity: the chosen alphabet length determines the maximum code space and code size.

## Request flows

Creation runs a single transaction: validate and normalize the submitted target as needed, allocate a code, insert the mapping, and return the short URL. An idempotency key can make client retries return the same created mapping after a network timeout. Bind that key to the authenticated principal and request parameters. Redirect is a point lookup by primary key. If the code exists and is active, return a 301 or 302 based on product semantics. Permanent caching with 301 can make destination changes difficult because clients and intermediaries may retain the redirect. A 302 or 307 offers more control; document the chosen behavior.

Validate allowed schemes such as HTTP and HTTPS to avoid turning the product into a dangerous `javascript:` redirect or an internal network proxy. Preview scanners and link unfurlers can trigger redirects; track bot traffic separately if analytics matter. Apply creation quotas and abuse detection for phishing, spam, and malware, while keeping moderation out of the latency-sensitive redirect path when possible.

## First scaling limits

On one machine, the database is both persistence and index. Add a cache only after observing read load; cache immutable or rarely changed mappings with a TTL and invalidation strategy. If destination edits are allowed, stale cached redirects need explicit handling. Use access logs or an asynchronous event queue for analytics. Back up the database and test restore. Measure lookup p95/p99, DB connection saturation, cache hit rate, creation failures, and redirect error rate.

Test duplicate code insertion, expired links, malformed URLs, a lost creation response followed by retry, database restart, and redirect caching. One machine is a valid first design when its capacity and recovery limits meet requirements. Keeping code allocation and uniqueness in the database makes later movement to multiple application servers straightforward; global uniqueness and analytics are the next design problems when scale demands them.

## Design review

What is the code allocation method and collision guard? Which redirect status code matches editability and caching? Are unsafe URL schemes rejected? Can analytics fail without breaking redirects? What traffic or recovery metric would trigger a move beyond one machine?

# Design: rate limiting and abuse prevention

Consider a public API that serves reads, creates expensive objects, and triggers downstream work. A single per-IP limit will not protect every cost or offer fair quotas. Build admission around distinct identities and resource budgets: anonymous traffic needs broad edge protection, authenticated users need account-level quotas, organizations need tenant budgets, and costly operations need stricter operation-specific limits. The service that owns each resource should enforce its own hard limit even when the gateway rejects most excess traffic earlier.

## Threat model and policy

Abuse ranges from credential stuffing and scraping to accidental retry storms and a customer integration with a bug. Identify the constrained resources: CPU, database reads, outbound API spend, queue depth, storage, and human review capacity. For each, set limits on rate, concurrency, payload size, and total allocation. Separate a burst allowance from a sustained rate. A token bucket lets a client use a limited burst while replenishing at a steady rate; a sliding window caps total actions in a rolling interval. Pick semantics that fit the product, then publish stable error responses and retry behavior.

Use several keys. The edge can count IP or network prefix before authentication, with generous thresholds for carrier NAT. After login, key by verified account or API credential. For SaaS, enforce a tenant ceiling so one organization cannot monopolize shared capacity. Add endpoint-class limits for high-cost operations and global circuit breakers for dependencies. Never derive identity from a caller-controlled header unless a trusted proxy strips and replaces it. Use a random API key identifier rather than the secret itself as a limiter key.

## Enforcement architecture

An API gateway performs cheap early rejection, coarse bot rules, payload-size limits, and global rate shaping. Application services enforce authorization-aware quotas and specific business limits. Workers enforce bounded concurrency and queue admission before expensive processing. Central shared state provides consistent counters across application replicas but adds network latency and failure modes. Atomic scripts or transactions prevent concurrent requests from double-spending quota. Local token buckets can protect the service during a shared-store outage, but the allowed fallback must be explicit; otherwise N local instances multiply the global limit by N.

Return `429 Too Many Requests` for caller quota exhaustion, with `Retry-After` when a safe estimate exists. Distinguish temporary overload from plan quota exhaustion if clients need different remediation. Do not expose whether a sensitive account exists through the limiter response. For internal overload, shed low-priority work, use deadlines, and bound retries. A queue only delays overload; cap its age and depth. Protect critical operations with reserved capacity so bulk jobs cannot starve login, checkout, or control-plane recovery.

## Abuse response and metrics

Use risk signals such as high failure rates, rapid account creation, unusual geography, repeated token guesses, or expensive request patterns. Automated blocking should include a recovery path for false positives. Rate limiting is not a substitute for authentication, input validation, fraud detection, or DDoS mitigation. Keep limit policy versioned, auditable, and adjustable without a code deploy where operationally useful.

Track admitted and denied traffic by operation, key class, tenant tier, and region; limiter latency and errors; queue age; downstream spend; and fallback mode. Test spoofed identity headers, many app instances, NAT users, account rotation, limiter store failure, and a sudden high-cost workload. Abuse prevention should protect shared service health while making fair, explainable decisions for legitimate users.

## Design review

Which resource does each limit protect? Where is identity verified? Are global, per-tenant, and per-operation budgets composed atomically? What happens during limiter-store failure? Can the response distinguish retryable load shedding from a durable quota limit?

# Design: a URL shortener at scale

At scale, a URL shortener is an asymmetric workload: creating a mapping is relatively rare, while redirects can be extremely frequent and geographically distributed. Keep the mapping immutable where possible, make reads cacheable, and move analytics off the redirect path. The architecture usually contains an API for creation, a durable mapping store, a distributed cache, a redirect service near users, and an asynchronous event pipeline for click analytics and abuse signals.

## Code generation and durable mapping

A relational sequence with base-62 encoding is simple but centralizes allocation. It can be partitioned into ranges or replaced by random codes as creation scales. Random allocation needs a uniqueness constraint and retry on collision. Snowflake-style IDs or preallocated ranges can reduce central calls, but reveal ordering or require clock and worker-ID coordination. Choose code length and entropy based on predictability, collision risk, and privacy. If codes are tenant-scoped or custom aliases are offered, uniqueness may be global or scoped; encode that rule in a unique index.

Persist `code → destination` as the source of truth with owner, lifecycle, policy state, and version. The redirect read path checks a hot cache first, then a replicated key-value or relational store. Cache popular mappings at the edge or regional layer. A viral code can become a hot key, so use CDN caching, request coalescing, or replicated cache entries. TTLs should respect expiration and update semantics. For immutable destinations, versioned cache entries and long TTLs are efficient. If destinations are editable or revoked, invalidation must propagate within a stated bound; high-risk revocation may require edge authorization on every hit or short-lived caching.

## Redirect correctness and abuse

A redirect request should remain minimal: parse a normalized code, retrieve a valid mapping, enforce status and expiry, and return a redirect. Keep target URLs bounded and restrict dangerous schemes. Use a status code whose cache behavior matches whether targets can change. Bot scanners and preview clients may fetch links automatically, so click analytics should distinguish likely human visits. Record click events asynchronously with a compact schema; the redirect response should not wait for analytics persistence. A durable queue or log can absorb bursts and replay events, while downstream consumers aggregate views, geography, and device classes.

Creation requires abuse controls: quotas, reputation, URL scanning, user reports, and rapid revocation. Avoid a full malware check synchronously if it makes creation unusable; place new links in a pending state or apply risk-based policy. Replicate mapping data across regions with an explicit consistency model. Creation may be strongly consistent at the home region while reads are eventually consistent elsewhere; if a brand-new link must work globally immediately, use read-through to the home region or route by code partition.

## Scale and operations

Shard by code hash or prefix for predictable lookup distribution, but popular keys may still concentrate cache traffic. Plan backup, restore, and deletion of expired links. Track redirect p99, cache hit ratio, hot-key skew, origin fallback, replication lag, event backlog, code collision retries, and unsafe-link reports. Test viral traffic, cache invalidation, a database region outage, duplicate click events, and a revoked destination still present in an edge cache.

## Design review

How are globally unique codes generated? What is the consistency contract for a new mapping? Can revocation reach cached redirects quickly? Does analytics failure affect redirect availability? How are viral hot keys and phishing reports handled?

# Design: a product listing

A product listing serves a browsable catalog with search, filters, sorting, and pagination. It combines product data that changes at different rates: names and descriptions, category membership, price, inventory, promotions, and media. A strong design assigns each field an authoritative owner, builds a read-optimized catalog view, and makes freshness tradeoffs explicit. The listing page should stay responsive even if one enrichment source is stale or unavailable.

## Separate writes from browse reads

The product service owns canonical product records and validation. Inventory and pricing often have separate write paths and freshness requirements. A change stream or transactional outbox publishes updates to a catalog index, search engine, and cache. The index is a derived read model, not the source of truth. It can denormalize category, brand, searchable text, filter fields, price ranges, and availability to avoid fanout queries at page-read time. Include a version or event sequence so stale events cannot overwrite newer documents. Rebuild the index from canonical stores and replay changes from a checkpoint.

For a small catalog, a relational database with indexes may support browse and filters adequately. At larger scale, a search engine can provide text relevance and faceted aggregations, while a relational or key-value store remains authoritative for updates. Search results can lag inventory or price updates, so the product page may recheck critical fields before checkout. If inventory accuracy is a purchase invariant, do not rely on an eventually consistent search document to guarantee stock; reserve inventory in its authoritative service during the purchase flow.

## Query, filters, and pagination

Define supported filters and sort orders before indexing. A combination of many optional facets can create expensive query shapes. Use bounded filter sets and precomputed facet counts where necessary. Facets should represent the current result set or explicitly indicate global counts; these are different semantics. Filter values must be normalized, and category hierarchy requires a clear parent-child model. Sorting by price needs stable tie-breaking so items do not jump unpredictably across pages.

Cursor pagination is usually safer than offset pagination for deep result sets. A cursor can carry the last sort tuple and index generation. Search results change while a user pages, so decide whether pagination is a live view or a snapshot. An index point-in-time snapshot gives stable pages but consumes resources; a live cursor is cheaper but may skip or repeat products after catalog updates. Cache popular category pages with a key that includes locale, currency, market, sort, filters, and catalog version as required. Do not cache user-specific price or entitlement data under a shared key.

## Availability and relevance

The listing path can degrade gracefully. If recommendation enrichment fails, return ranked catalog results; if inventory data is stale, label it or prevent a strong availability promise. Relevance can combine text match, business rules, popularity, personalization, and availability, but each component should have bounded latency and a fallback. Monitor index lag, query p95/p99, no-result rate, filter use, stale price reports, cache hit rate, and conversion by query class. Avoid using click-through alone as a quality metric because position bias can reinforce existing rankings.

Test concurrent product edits, delayed or duplicate events, zero-result filters, changing inventory between pages, locale-specific currency, and a full index rebuild. A listing design succeeds when users can find the right product quickly while critical purchase facts are revalidated by their system of record.

## Design review

Which service owns each catalog field? How does the read model recover from missed events? Are filter and sort combinations bounded? Does pagination promise a stable snapshot? Which attributes are safe to cache globally, and when are price and inventory rechecked?

# Design: a collaborative editor

A collaborative editor must make local typing feel immediate while several users edit the same document, possibly from offline devices. Separate the document's durable shared content from ephemeral presence such as cursors and typing indicators. Choose a merge model that fits document semantics and product guarantees: operational transformation (OT) commonly orders and transforms operations through a central authority, while conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) let replicas merge concurrent updates according to defined algebraic rules. Neither choice removes the need to design persistence, authorization, history, and resource limits.

## Data and synchronization model

Represent the document as structured nodes or shared text rather than a single HTML string if users need concurrent rich-text edits. Client edits should apply locally first for low perceived latency, then send operations or CRDT updates to the collaboration service. The service authenticates the user, checks room access, validates document and update size, persists accepted updates, and broadcasts them to connected collaborators. Presence messages use a separate short-lived channel because losing a cursor update must not lose a content edit. Awareness state should expire when a client disconnects and should not be retained as document history.

With OT, a server sequences operations and transforms incoming edits against operations already accepted. It provides a natural place to order writes but creates a central sequencing dependency and requires careful version handling. With CRDTs, replicas exchange state or incremental updates that can merge despite different arrival orders; offline edits can sync later, but metadata and tombstones may grow, and garbage collection or compaction must preserve merge correctness. Pick a mature, tested implementation rather than improvising transformation logic. Define the ordering and behavior for overlapping insertions, deletion versus formatting, and rich-text structural conflicts.

## Persistence and scale

The hot collaboration path can use WebSockets to deliver updates, with a document room or shard owning in-memory state. Persist updates to an append-only log or database before acknowledging durable success, or explicitly distinguish accepted-in-memory from saved. Periodically create snapshots so reconnecting clients need not replay an unbounded history. A durable update log enables recovery after room-owner loss. Assign each room to an owner for ordering and local batching; route clients consistently, and rebalance rooms without losing acknowledged updates. Very large popular documents may require partitioning or flow control, but splitting one shared sequence can complicate ordering.

Offline clients keep local updates and submit them after reconnect. The server should validate authorization again because permissions may have changed while offline. Updates should be idempotent by operation identity or CRDT update semantics. Retain version history through snapshots plus later updates, and define restore behavior: restoring a snapshot while users are active is a new merge or branch, not simply replacing bytes. Apply quotas for document size, update rate, connected sessions, and fanout to protect shared rooms.

Measure update-to-peer latency, local-to-durable acknowledgment, reconnect recovery time, room fanout, snapshot age, rejected updates, and document growth. Test partitions, duplicate update delivery, simultaneous edits at one position, permission revocation, owner crash, and a client reconnecting from a long-offline state. The editor is correct only if visible content converges and acknowledged edits survive failure.

## Design review

Why choose OT or CRDT for these document semantics? Are content and presence separated? When is an edit considered durable? How does an offline client reauthorize and reconcile? Can a room recover from its owner without losing acknowledged changes?
